Day two: https://stacker.news/items/1603699

Thanks for reading and following along!

items.title: In Search of Freedom: Life, Death, and Sovereignty in the Himalaya
items.text:
![](https://m.stacker.news/164458)

*I’m sitting in a dusty hotel room in Kathmandu, attempting to call a Spanish airline about my missing luggage.*
*“We’ll have to email our ground staff contractor,” they say.*
*I try to protest. “My trek starts tomorrow!”*
*“Please check your email later today, sir.”*
*I listen to the click of the agent hanging up the phone.*

The hotel is nestled precisely in the middle of Thamel, the tourist district with its colourful flags, rooftop gardens, and too-narrow streets. There is plenty to do in the capital, but after three days of chasing my lost bag in a Kafkaesque system of virtual shrugs and missed callbacks, my energy wanes. I am trapped in the antipresent, unable to visit any tourist attractions, only capable of reconnecting to the hotel WiFi to refresh my emails for the 800th time in the hope of news. With nothing but time, I feel utterly trapped.

During a 2018 volunteering trip to Nepal, I waited for my opportunity to walk the Annapurna Circuit: a two-week hiking route crossing high paths and winding through tiny Buddhist villages. Instead, I got a call to fly back to the UK. My father had been diagnosed with bowel cancer, and it was terminal. He was the one who introduced me to hiking, taught me to be patient when faced with another false peak, to understand the swirling patterns of clouds, to clean my kit, to be prepared for sudden change, to appreciate in the silence of the wilderness, to be present. Near the end, we talked a lot about hiking.

“When you see a mountain,” he said, “think of me.”
I can’t remember what I said in return.

It took eight years to get back to Nepal — grief, travel, COVID, relocation, work, money, rule changes, and procrastination saw to that. After all my posturing about being an advocate for freedom, living my life exactly how I wanted, my fear of closure held me back. I wouldn’t gain perspective until I’d seen those mountains again.

***

![](https://m.stacker.news/164459)

*Finally, after another two-day delay, I take the first steps of my 18-day trek. The Manang Valley bathes in bright sunlight. We pass apple orchards and fields of buckwheat as we climb to Lower Pisang, but after nearly a week stuck in the hotel, I feel like I could run up the path for hours. I’m not doing this alone; there are ten in my group — other travellers looking for answers in the hills. We get to know each other in the brief moments when we’re not gasping for breath in the thinning air.*

That night, I fire up my Kindle and read [*The Ones Who Walk Away From Omelas*](https://shsdavisapes.pbworks.com/f/Omelas.pdf). It’s one of my all-time favourites, a short story that’s more of a thought experiment. Ursula Le Guin presents a Utopian society of harmony, peace, and joy. In Omelas, life is wonderful for every resident except one: a miserable child, suffering alone in a dungeon. Most residents can ignore the one person whose incarceration guarantees their joy and freedom, but the few who can’t leave the citadel forever.

Maybe it’s hubris, but I’ve always considered myself one of those who ‘walk away’. I’ve been willing to give up convenience to claw back some of the sovereignty I’d lost through a corporate job and living in a mediocre London suburb. And here I was on a legendary remote hiking route, perhaps not scaling peaks, but at least challenging myself, climbing higher than I’ve ever been.

***

![](https://m.stacker.news/164462)

*The nights are cold at 4000m above sea level, and my wardrobe is more suited to the Spanish summer than sub-zero temperatures. As we hike farther up, across metal suspension bridges and past well-insulated herds of yaks, I wear my father’s old gear — a down vest and the bright red* *waterproof. It’s not a homage; it’s purely practical. Still, it gives me some kind of connection.*

I feel him silently judging me for walking the ‘tourist trail’. He always had to plan the route and bring every bit of kit himself, while a Nepalese porter carries my luggage strapped directly to their forehead. He would also have loved seeing the world’s highest peaks up close and listening to the guides' explanations of the dangers, the routes, the climbers. We all live the battle of comfort vs sovereignty.

The ‘tea house’ hotels in the Manang valley have a few more mod cons than expected. Some even have hot showers. But today, the power for the whole village is out. As the sun sets, my roommate and I read by the light of our headtorches.

Before the trip, I’d just finished reading *The Gulag Archipelago*, Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn’s brutal account of the anti-freedoms of Communist Russia. That night, I search for a quote that jumped off the page when I read it: ‘All those years in our cells and our huts, the state’s electricity had seared our souls, and now, darkness was bliss.’ Sometimes, our only freedom comes through stoic minimalism and absence. I turned off my reading light and listened to the darkness.

***

![](https://m.stacker.news/164463)

*I’m in bed with a worsening cold. The lack of doctors and pharmacies doesn’t seem so quaint when you are coughing up your lungs. The 5,416m Thorong La Pass plays on my mind, and I struggle to sleep. It’s not just me; another member of the group has a virus, and most of the others are blowing their runny noses in the dry mountain air. We take each day slowly, climbing 500m in altitude, and putting one foot in front of the other. There aren’t any other options: turning back involves walking too, and I don’t like going backwards.*

By this point, we’ve walked 80km or so. [Karl Bushby](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq8rz38jr50go) has just finished walking 50,000km after circumnavigating the globe by foot. I watched a video on his trip just before setting off on mine, and I was most impressed by the fact he had no desire to break records, no charity campaign, no press team. “Every fibre of my being,” he says, “every day, has been what I'm doing right now.”

Along the way, between icy paths and sneezes, I hit upon the idea that walking is trustless. That’s why it is so freeing to Karl Bushby and to all of us. You don’t rely on anyone or anything else. It is the rhythm of taking one step at a time. Sometimes things go as expected; sometimes they don't. But freedom is not about control. It depends on adapting to your surroundings and being in sync with the path. Each day, the tea houses serve another group of foreigners. Monks in the small temples perform another ceremony, another meditation. The kitchens produce another hundred plates of dal bhat, accompanied by ginger tea for the sniffling guests. The sun rises over snowy peaks again.

One of the guys in our group walked to Everest Base Camp more than 20 years ago. Things were quite primitive back then. He told me the soundtrack of those two weeks was the constant *thunk* of cattle bells. That was his rhythm, his surroundings. He bought a heavy metal bell in a Kathmandu market at the end of his trip and still displays it proudly in his New Jersey house.

***

![](https://m.stacker.news/164464)

*It’s 4 am and -15℃ on the day we climb over the pass and down the other side. Lines of headtorches light the steep path up, and the snow crunches under boots fitted with temporary metal spikes. The path ahead is backed up because a girl from another group has fainted. Her partner attempts to carry her up on piggyback, but stops after just a few steps.*

*As we wait for the last members of our party to arrive, we hop from foot to foot to keep warm. Frank, a German realtor who lives in Cape Town, excitedly tells us he has the WiFi password for a teahouse we’ve just passed. ‘Who cares?’ I think. ‘You’ve flown all the way here to cross this pass, and you’ve gotten up in the dark to do it. Why do you need WiFi?’*

Later, after the girl who collapsed has passed us riding on a yak, after we’ve taken our photos at the top, and after we’ve descended to 3,800 meters and bathed in the sun of the afternoon, I reflect on Frank and his need for WiFi passwords. Yes, we are all plugged into our digital worlds, but if you can’t spend a few hours away from it, are you really free at all?

I think about the amount of time I spent that day completely disconnected, staring at the contrast of birds of prey crossing white peaks and soaring up into a blue sky. Why do we struggle to think beyond the next unit of time? The next breath, photo, coffee break, the next day, the next WiFi access point. Why do we need to extract immediate value from our physical world?

I can’t always rein in my differences from the group. Not everyone has waited eight long years to reconnect with their father by climbing a Nepalese mountain. This is every fibre of my being, not just a social media photo op. My father would have loved to build a homestead, to fix machines, grow cattle, and walk the land, but he chose a secure life so his children could do that.

The next days we pass through small towns celebrating *Dashain* — a time for families, giving thanks, and taking stock. We stay with a local family and experience life in a small town; while we eat set meals and walk to a strict schedule, it feels like all the Nepalis around us are making their own choices.

We watch old ladies harvesting millet and corn. Heavy machinery continues to shift the earth of roads and riverbanks affected by landslides. We see new entrepreneurs opening restaurants, tea houses, and local stores. I speak to Ram, one of our guides, who is working through the festival period to put his kids through college in Japan. Everyone must hustle to improve their lot because saving in Rupees is futile. Even with remittances from those working abroad, Nepal is constantly playing catch-up. Everyone is building a better life here; no one expects it to be easy.

***

![](https://m.stacker.news/164466)

*My final day is spent in Kathmandu. A few of us travel to Durbar Square to see the world’s only living goddess. The Kumari is a young girl selected from a northern village. There are strict physical and mental tests as well as a birthdate that matches specific astrological criteria. She is taken from her parents to live in an opulent palace, where her feet may never touch the ground below. If she sheds a drop of blood, she is cast out into the realm of the mortals and is replaced by a new Kumari. Hindus and Buddhists alike come to see her, hoping to be blessed by one of her three daily appearances at her palace window. The current Kumari is just three years old. After waiting an hour for her to appear, I feel like her nervous little wave is an anticlimax. The crowd still gasps.*

Later, it hits me that she is the living embodiment of the child in *The Ones Who Walk Away from Omelas*. Instead of being tortured or in pain, she is doted on. She has expensive gowns, extravagant makeup, a team of handlers, tutors, and adoring fans, but she is cursed. Her childhood is stolen, and she is imprisoned to bring others luck, joy, and religious harmony. She cannot play, shout, hide, misbehave, cry, laugh, or neglect her duties. She cannot walk where she pleases. To tourists, the Kumari is a sweet anomaly, a curious tradition. To Nepalis, she is a living goddess. Almost everyone is happy with this arrangement.

![](https://m.stacker.news/164460)

I went to Nepal to reconnect with emotions I had long since buried. Curiously, I saw glimpses of freedom instead of apparitions of my father. Sometimes I saw them in the hawks cruising high above, sometimes in the industrious lives of locals, and sometimes in the restrictions of those trapped in digital worlds or religious constructs.

If there is one thing I learned on this journey across the Annapurna mountains, it is that freedom is gained one step at a time. You have to know which direction you are heading, and you must understand what you are leaving behind.

items.title: I finally visited Pubkey in Washington DC
items.text:
![](https://m.stacker.news/162019)

I am attending a reunion of sorts of some old friends in DC.  I had some free time yesterday, so I finally got the opportunity to visit the Washington Pubkey.

I have posted a few times about the NYC version. I have a great time whenever I go:

https://stacker.news/items/219987/r/siggy47

https://stacker.news/items/230440/r/siggy47

https://stacker.news/items/1283387/r/siggy47

The Washington DC version of Pubkey is located on 7th Street in the [Penn Quarter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penn_Quarter) neighborhood of the city. It's not far from Ford's Theater and the J Edgar Hoover FBI building.  Capital One Arena, where the Washington Capitals play, is down the block. It is an upscale, touristy location.

Pubkey DC opened in January, 2026, according to the website, but I thought it had been around longer.  Yesterday the Washington Capitals had an early game, so there were plenty of fans in jerseys milling about. When I walked in I immediately noticed how different this place was from the New York version. It's huge, around 12,000 square feet, with two bars, a stage, and big screens everywhere showing sporting events. There was a good crowd, which looked to be a mix of tourists, locals, and hockey fans. I can't be certain, but I'm pretty sure I was the only person in the place interested in bitcoin.

This is not an in your face bitcoin space. I had just had a long car and was hungry. I decided to sit at the bar and have some lunch after exploring a bit.

At first I didn't notice much bitcoin stuff, but it is all strategically placed to fit in unobtrusively. I liked the low key design. It could be any sports /tourist spot in any city.

There were a few stickers in the men's room:

![](https://m.stacker.news/162028)

![](https://m.stacker.news/162029)

I then noticed a large wall display with some actively mining bitaxes:

![](https://m.stacker.news/162030)

And this small, but intriguing stack of bitcoin and bitcoin adjacent books below a "Free Samourai" sign:

![](https://m.stacker.news/162032)

I sat at the bar and saw this cool display:

![](https://m.stacker.news/162033)

Occasionally the ticker had a news flash scrolling across the screen.

When ordering my lunch I let the bartender know that I planned to pay in bitcoin. I was told that if I did, I would receive a 21% discount, which is impressive. I asked about the payment setup, and was a little disappointed that they just use square. I tried to.engage my server in a little bitcoin banter, but it was obvious he had no deep interest. I dont want to sound negative. All of the workers were friendly and competent. The menu was similar to the NYC Pubkey. I had a Caesar wrap, which was very good.  I must say paying with the square app was quick and easy. You select the tip amount before the invoice is generated, which is nice. I have experienced a few awkward moments trying to tip at the NYC Pubkey. You never can be sure if the server would prefer sats or dollars. This way they probably get a choice.

That being said, paying with square is still disappointing.

On the way out I found this board near the front bar:

![](https://m.stacker.news/162036)

I guess this proves there are some bitcoiners patronizing the place.

I didn't get to experience an event, but there is plenty of room for bitcoin gatherings. NYC Pubkey always feels a little cramped. I know Thomas Massie will be holding a discussion soon. I hope I get some time on my next trip to catch a presentation.

Why should we have to wait for online stores to accept Bitcoin before we can actually use it? ⚡

Millions of people shop online every day, yet most e-commerce stores still don't accept Bitcoin.

But what if the solution isn't convincing merchants to accept Bitcoin, but changing the way we shop?

That's the idea behind Bitpost.

We've built a peer-to-peer marketplace that connects two types of people:

🟠 People who want to spend Bitcoin to buy products online.

🟠 People who want to stack Bitcoin by purchasing those products on someone else's behalf using traditional payment methods, and receiving BTC in return.

No merchant integrations required. No need for online stores to accept Bitcoin directly.

We started with Amazon to validate the concept, but our vision goes much further.

Our goal is to make Bitcoin spendable across any e-commerce store, without depending on merchants to adopt it.

Bitpost is already live in its first version.

We've seen strong interest from people who want to stack sats through this model.

Now we're looking for the other side: people who actually want to spend Bitcoin.

Because we believe Bitcoin shouldn't just be something you hold. It should also be something you have the freedom to use.

So here's our question for the Bitcoin community:

If you could shop at any online store using Bitcoin, even when that store doesn't accept BTC, would you?

And more importantly, what would make you trust and try a service like this?

We're genuinely interested in your ideas, concerns, and honest criticism.

🌐 https://www.bitpost.shop

The future of shopping with Bitcoin shouldn't have to wait for merchants to catch up.⚡

# 2024 - snickerbar.me

For Halloween of 2024, I had been experimenting with ecash and was having a blast with stacker.news. I decided to pass out ecash tokens to the parents of trick or treaters to encourage bitcoin adoption in our neighborhood. I forked cashu.me and engaged in some coding that was way over my head and mostly a learning experience for me. The results varied from "eh" to "aight" and fun was had by all. I chronicled that spooky season in [a post exposing my coding ineptitude](https://stacker.news/items/717596), [making a spooky crossword puzzle for stackers](https://stacker.news/items/723313), [iterating](https://stacker.news/items/729712), [mashing up Janet Yellen and Metallica to @DarthCoin's delight](https://stacker.news/items/748546), and ultimately [passing out small amount of sats while playing music by David Lynch on a DX-7](https://stacker.news/items/748618).

![](https://m.stacker.news/56707)

![](https://m.stacker.news/60570)

It was a fun time.

# 2025 - They don't celebrate Halloween in Mossel Bay

South African townships have witches. I never met one, but I heard quite a bit about them, and sadly, it was mostly from scared children. I've been told that the witches are responsible for gangs, substance abuse, and general violence in the townships. What was very sad to me was the amount of talismans I saw children wearing to "protect" themselves from witches. There is a very real bondage there, and as I was in Mossel Bay for Halloween 2025, we kept it low key and at home.

My wife and I personally do believe that there is a supernatural realm, but are thoroughly convinced that talismans, incantations, and other charms do nothing to protect people from evil. So, at home, we kept our American traditions, which are solely for fun and pretend. We made costumes out of paper. The kids did trick or treat to the rooms my wife and I separated to in the two bedroom apartment. We used what was available to make little jack 'o lanterns.

![](https://m.stacker.news/163859)

And in doing so, almost burnt the place down.

![](https://m.stacker.news/163860)

If you're wondering, no, I do not recommend at this point that you fill a gem squash with kerosene soaked fire starters.

We finished the night with some kid-friendly spooky stories. Alas, last Halloween featured no caramel apples, no hayrides, no corn mazes, and worst of all, NO ECASH!

# 2026 - Making up for lost time

The mills of God have done their dance, and now I can...VIBE CODE! What that translates to is a whole new level of usability of this free ecash for my neighbors. Here is [https://snickerbar-me.vercel.app/](https://snickerbar-me.vercel.app/) for 2026. 

Tonight is Trunk or Treat, and boy-howdy, do I have a treat in my trunk.

![](https://m.stacker.news/163863)

![](https://m.stacker.news/163874)

items.title: Austin trip day one: Bitcoin all around
items.text:
Evening stackers,

I write from my hotel having just checked in and showered after a very long productive day.

I landed in Austin at 1045 AM and I had rented a Turo. It took me a frustratingly long time to find the damn thing but once I was was in the right garage (blue  not red) I found it pretty quickly. Then I went to my hotel, a grungy little thing 15 min south of round rock, only to be told I couldn’t check in for another 1.5 hours. I was looking forward to a shower and a nap before heading out to meet @Scoresby at PlebLab. No matter, the poker room The Lodge Poker Club was only a 13 min drive away. I could kill some time there no problem.

![](https://m.stacker.news/163462)

![](https://m.stacker.news/163463)

![](https://m.stacker.news/163464)

The place was really nice inside with plenty of tables and friendly staff. After getting my players account all set up  I waited for 20 min or so to get seated at a 1/2 500 max no limit Texas Holdem game.

The game was good and the players were friendly. I posted a breakdown of my favorite hand in the saloon here:

https://stacker.news/items/1602411/r/SatAttack?commentId=1602968

They had a table of treats for sale perhaps made staff member and I am sucker for both pastries and supporting small business so—win win. I got the pumpkin spice cake with cream cheese frosting (delicious). Here it is:

![](https://m.stacker.news/163465)

I only played for 1.5 hours and instead of going to the hotel to check in I headed straight to town to meet with @scoresby and @k00b which I was a bit nervous about. I’m not a very social person. But I was doubly excited to not only meet some real life bitcoiners, but fellow stackers! The pm stackers who created and build this place no less ! So off I went, nerves be damned. 

I found PlebLab easy enough. It’s a cool small space with ultimate hacker vibes. Scoresby and Koob came to say hey right away and were very cool and friendly. Koob wasn’t wearing any shoes, which is apparently normal for him, and as a fellow barefoot person, I give triple salute. Shoes suck. I’ve been a barefoot person my whole life and I too am barefoot at work every day. Kudos to Koob. He gave me some cool SN stickers and a cooler SN hat and pretty quickly Scoresby and I embarked on a city walk. I wish I would have thanked Koob for his founding and effort for curating this Bitcoin internet social for all of us but sadly I forgot.

It was very very cool talking to scoresby, what a guy. We had a lot of bitcoin related things to talk about which is so (pardon my French) fucking refreshing man. This is rare for me. Maybe for you too, dear reader. To be able to talk to a bitcoiner about bitcoin is so much fun. We can jump to this conclusion or that realization because we understand exactly where we are coming from in certain outlooks, opinions, knowledge, and world views. Scoresby is the man. He took me all around and showed me where there has been some awesome sounding Bitcoin events in the past. He showed me where the unchained head quarters is. He took me to Waller beach where walked along the Colorado River for a good ways. He showed me a bridge where apparently millions of bats live and come out at night in huge swarms. We could hear them chittering away. We saw a turtle. We saw a woman chatting on the phone in the grass with a HODL shirt on. Cool to see out in the wild, we both agreed.

He was quite curious about my poker playing and if someone is asking my about poker I have a hard time noticing anything else. So my recollection of surrounding details on the trail is a bit shoddy. I can rant and rant on that topic. I had a great time chatting it up and really appreciated his time taking me around. I loved talking and breathing bitcoin like it was a normal part of every day life. I felt submersed in its community just by chatting it up. We talked about the direction he would like SN to go and his efforts to make it happen. We spoke about current security incidents, cold storage options, SN sending wallet option past and present cultural shifts… it was great. Often I feel like I am the only real life bitcoiner out there when I’m surrounded by people who don’t know or don’t care but here in this moment, I felt the opposite. Perhaps it was the combination of being in a new city, talking to a new person, and seeing new things, but it felt like bitcoinization has already happened. It was normalized. We were the normal ones…

After an hour of walking we parted ways and it was time for me to EAT.

@plebpoet had suggested I go to a BBQ place called The Green Mesquite. “The real ones” go there she said. So not wanting to risk being a shoeby, that’s where I went.

![](https://m.stacker.news/163466)

![](https://m.stacker.news/163467)

Now the first thing I deeply appreciated was they had their own parking lot!! If you’ve ever been to Austin you know that parking here may be the only thing comparatively scarce to Bitcoin. The place has a real Texas saloon vibe to it and I thought just maybe this place has been here just as long as Austin. The man at the counter was friendly and had me sit anywhere. There was only one other person there. There were lots of old Texas decorations and Older country and blue grass songs playing which I appreciated. (Don’t like this new stuff in that genre)

I quickly decided that the best route would be a BBQ platter so I could try as many different things as possible. I went with the three meat choice and got smoked brisket, dark meat chicken, and sausage. My sides were green beans and fried okra and I got a shiner bock to wash it down with. Here it is:

![](https://m.stacker.news/163469)

Everything was delicious. I don’t know WHAT is going on with their BBQ sauce, sitting unceremoniously and unlabeled with all the other condiments, but it was amazing. It wasn’t crazy sweet and complimented the chicken and brisket so very well. I didn’t try on the sausage as I didn’t feel the need. It was so juicy and flavorful.

As I’m sitting finishing my beer something really wonderful happened. I saw a man through the window walking up, dirty and skinny and disheveled. He came through the door and I was too far to hear the words exchanged but I’m fairly certain he asked for a meal and said he couldn’t pay for it. Without anger or hesitation the guy working the counter said “I can do a sausage roll” and made him a small meal. The roll, some chips, and a water.

It was really wholesome and I can honestly say I’ve never seen anything like it.

I left shortly after and sat in my car and pulled up BTCmaps to see what sort of trouble I could get myself into. Just 7 min drive away there was a place listed called Local Pastures. Here is their BTCmap and website:

[https://btcmap.org/merchant/node:10791261306](https://btcmap.org/merchant/node:10791261306)

[https://www.localpastures.farm](https://www.localpastures.farm)

![](https://m.stacker.news/163470)

![](https://m.stacker.news/163471)

![](https://m.stacker.news/163472)

![](https://m.stacker.news/163473)

These guys are awesome! It’s a tiny little store the size of a large Kobe’s box and they get local meats, dairy’s, produce, and coffee and sell them here. When I walked in the first thing I noticed was their square terminal. They have the flip version. I poked around for maybe only a minute before asking the man if they accept bitcoin and he said “yep no problem.” Ha! Another victory for the books. Now it’s time to shop. Unfortunately the majority of their stuff required a kitchen to get use out of but the selection was quite nice. I had to settle for snacks. I got a couple of beef sticks and some pecans by two separate local farms.

![](https://m.stacker.news/163474)

When it was time to ring up he remembered I wanted to pay with sats and pretty quickly generated a lightning invoice before flipping it over to me. Easy day. Phoenix wallet again didn’t disappoint in speed and success. I asked him if he had ever heard of BTCmaps and he said no. I let him know that’s how I found this image and gave a brief explanation about what it is. He thought it was pretty cool when I showed him. I also asked if anyone else spends bitcoin there he said maybe once a month. He did say that for some stretch of time in the past there was a guy who would come 1-2 times a week and spend his sats there but he moved away. Perhaps that guy is a stacker. 

We had spoke a bit back at PlebLab about how disappointing BTCmaps can be. It definitely does not paint an accurate picture of where you can find places to spend your hard earned sats. So it felt good to get one first try. Maybe I’m lucky? Maybe I have a knack for finding the spots? Really I just liked that this one had a carrot as their symbol on the map and it was conveniently close by.

All in all, great day. I will now take a quick power nap and head back to the poker room for a couple hours of table time.

Day two post coming tomorrow!

My final preparations are coming together to present a catalog of SNZ issues to the general zine-making public alongside my poetry book published last summer. I submitted SNZ early this year to be considered for showing and was accepted. I paid $20 for half of a table where I'll sit from 12 to 6 on Saturday, hopefully not receiving shunning or shaming for being an artist interested in bitcoin. I expect to have interesting conversations meeting and mingling with the other creators. My read of the sentiment amongst artists in Austin is one that is not really cozy with technology as a means to a hopeful future (but I don't *really* know). If that is exactly what I get to spend the day talking about, I'm gonna be super happy with that.

Beyond that, if I have the chance to show off Stacker News, why I like it, why I use bitcoin, and all things of that nature, I will be delighted!

![](https://m.stacker.news/160737)

I'll be selling the zines and books using a Cashapp business account that allows my phone to become a tap-to-pay terminal for cards. I haven't used this feature before, and it does seem a little fantastical. Would be absolutely magic to me if that works. I don't have high expectations for meeting a potential customer that wants to pay in bitcoin, but if that should be the case, I'm ready to accept bitcoin over lightning through Cashapp as well.

# Stacker input wanted

The table setting I'm putting together is *out of this world*:
![](https://m.stacker.news/160738)

We have exactly what I think should be there, nothing more. It's not gonna be crowded out or loaded down. There's a QR code to my website, there's a price sheet, stacker news stickers for free, and the merch.

I should perhaps include a QR to SN. I don't know how often people casually pursue a QR code though, is there a better presentation/representation for SN generally? OR are there specific talking points about SN that you've had success with? Let me know.
My thinking is to speak only from my experience, share that up front and also admit I don't know everything. THANKS
yours truly,
plebpoet

items.title: Introducing PayPerQ's (PPQ.AI) new Enclave Router privacy architecture
items.text:
Hey guys, I'm Matt, founder of PayPerQ (PPQ.AI), the pay-per-use AI router that gives a 5% bonus for lightning deposits. We shipped a big privacy upgrade yesterday that I believe is worthy of a post over here.

Every chat through PPQ now runs inside an AWS Nitro enclave that proves two things:

1. PPQ **cannot read the content of your queries**.
2. PPQ **sent your query to the model and provider you actually picked.** No model fraud.

![](https://m.stacker.news/160721)

Every AI router out there, us included until yesterday, can read the prompts going through it. "We don't log your prompts" has only ever been a promise.


Now the only thing we see is billing and error metadata. The enclave code is open source and reproducibly built, and we shipped a small local verifier you can run so you don't have to trust us or Amazon on it.


Combine that with no accounts and paying in sats, and the provider that can read your prompt has no idea who you are, while PPQ, which knows how you paid, can't read your prompt.

Honest caveat: this covers chat only for now. Image, video and audio still hit our backend directly. And frontier providers like Anthropic still see your prompt because that's where the model runs.

Full writeup: [https://ppq.ai/blog/introducing-the-enclave-router](https://ppq.ai/blog/introducing-the-enclave-router)
The thread version: [https://x.com/PPQdotAI/status/2107875352420970878](https://x.com/PPQdotAI/status/2107875352420970878)
Code: [https://github.com/PayPerQ/ppq-enclave-proxy](https://github.com/PayPerQ/ppq-enclave-proxy)

Happy to answer any questions here. Hopefully we are staying true to our users' expectations with regard to freedom, privacy, and sovereignty.

items.title: Bitcoin Stablecoins and the Freedom to Choose
items.text:
After attending bitcoin++ Berlin, payments edition, two talks have been stuck in my head.

Allen Farrington’s [The Fiat Payment Stack Returns (Part 2), The Sequel](https://btcpp.dev/berlin26#berlin26_fiat_bf4b) explored how complicated fiat payments are underneath the familiar experience of tapping a card.

Then Lightrider’s [It Worked on My Node](https://btcpp.dev/berlin26#berlin26_worked_c209) showed us real numbers from nadanada.me. Once they added credit cards, Monero, shitcoins, and stablecoins, Bitcoin payments became a minority. And lightning is now just 10% of their payments.

Cryptorefills’ checkout data tells a similar story: stablecoins overtook Bitcoin in 2021 and now account for roughly two thirds of completed purchases on its platform.

![](https://m.stacker.news/160195)

I recommend watching both when the recordings are published. Together, they left me with an uncomfortable thought: the payment system we want to replace is a mess, yet people still aren’t choosing ours. I think we should take that seriously.

Bitcoin is a miracle. We have scarce digital money that we can hold under our own keys, without a bank deciding whether we deserve access. Nobody gets to print more. That is extraordinary.

We have won something enormous: the ability to save outside the banking system. I remain very bullish. Bitcoin is volatile, but my bet over the long run is still up and to the right.

But we haven’t won everyday payments. And perhaps we’ve spent too much time treating those as the same problem.

You might be happy to hold bitcoin through volatility. But a merchant trying to pay wages and suppliers may not be. Accepting bitcoin and wanting to keep bitcoin are different decisions. Meanwhile, a customer’s card is familiar, costs nothing to the user, and works everywhere.

If they choose that, it's not because they are "dumb". They’re solving their problems.

If we believe in free markets, the market gets to disagree with us. We should be curious about what people want, and build something worth choosing.

There is plenty to improve. Visa and Mastercard payments involve issuers, acquirers, processors, networks, currency conversion, and reconciliation. Merchants pay for that machinery, and the fees hurt when margins are thin. International transfers can be worse: in the third quarter of 2025, sending a $200 remittance cost 6.36% on average globally. Almost $13 just to move $200.

![](https://m.stacker.news/160191)

Stablecoins give people something immediately useful: familiar money that can move over an open network. For someone with an unstable local currency, limited banking access, or customers abroad, a digital dollar can solve a real problem today. Just like Bitcoin, but with less volatility.

Yes, stablecoins are fiat squared. You inherit fiat’s problems and add an issuer who can fail, restrict redemption, or freeze your tokens. But people are comparing them with the bank accounts and payment services they actually have. We should do the same.

I’m also unconvinced that CBDCs are the inevitable future. Several early launches have struggled to attract meaningful use. Governments can launch a product; they can’t manufacture a reason to want it.

My bet is that stablecoins will become the dominant way money moves across the internet, eventually taking over much of what card networks do today. People may still tap cards. Visa and Mastercard may adapt and thrive. The interface can stay familiar while the money underneath changes.

I often see Paolo Ardoino depicted as evil in Bitcoin circles. I don't know if he is. But what matters is whether he is right about stablecoins. And he might be.

Which brings me to the part that excites me: those dollars could move over Lightning.

What's the best "house" for stablecoins? There are many blockchains available. And looks like Tron is winning. Then Ethereum, Solana, Binance, ... So it's not like their users appreciate security and decentralization the most. Running a full node for any of those requires expensive equipment. Apart from other issues like PoS and even shittier version of that that give control to a handful or operators. But they are cheap. Big blocks, coming out every few seconds.

![](https://m.stacker.news/160192)

![](https://m.stacker.news/160194)

But blockchains don't scale. So if the whole world population would be using stablecoins, none of those would be able to keep up. At least without becoming a centralized database which might be too much even for the most careless shitcoiners.

But we have already solved that! No blockchain will be ever capable of competing with a channel based payments network like lightning. In terms of throughput and fees. So maybe Lightning is the best "house" for stablecoins after all.

Payment channels let us make many payments without recording every one on a global ledger. Bitcoin provides the foundation, while payments happen across a network of channels. I think that is a powerful architecture for global payments.

With Taproot Assets, a dollar payment can be exchanged into bitcoin at one edge, routed through Lightning, and exchanged into the recipient’s asset at the other. The customer can spend dollars. The merchant can receive dollars. Bitcoin can connect them without either having to share our monetary convictions.

Somebody has to provide liquidity and make the exchanges worthwhile. But the architecture is real. Tether has announced plans to bring USDt to Bitcoin and Lightning through Taproot Assets. I think we should be paying attention.

And honestly once on Lightning, the interoperability of Taproot assets with real bitcoin makes it too easy to switch. So that's another win there. Would be way easier to go from stablecoins to bitcoin than from fiat in a bank account to bitcoin, which is the current baseline.

![](https://m.stacker.news/160193)

The difficult part will be making it pleasant to use.

Self-custodial Lightning still involves channels, liquidity, backups, and recovery. We can improve that experience, but wishing everyone would run their own infrastructure won’t make it happen.

Some people will choose a provider. Others will want their own keys. Tools like Cashu offer another useful possibility: private ecash, backed by a mint the user trusts. That involves custody, but can offer privacy that an ordinary payment account doesn’t.

I can imagine wallets, mints, and payment companies connected through Lightning, competing to serve people who want to spend different kinds of money. What matters is whether users can move between them, withdraw their funds, recover from mistakes, and take more control when they want to.

Max Hillebrand’s *The Praxeology of Privacy* helped me think about this. I take from it an emphasis on practical progress toward autonomy. We don’t have to wait for everyone to adopt our ideal setup before helping them become freer.

Freedom comes before Bitcoin.

Bitcoin matters because of what it lets people do. If someone wants dollars for spending, I want to help them use dollars with lower costs, better privacy, and more choice. If they later want sovereign savings, Bitcoin should be within reach. The immediate benefit should be theirs, not our satisfaction at having converted another person.

I might be wrong about stablecoins winning, or Lightning becoming their best network. The honest way to find out is to listen, build, and compete.

Bitcoin has given people an extraordinary way to save. Now let’s give them better ways to spend, with useful wallets, private payments, and services they can leave as easily as they can join.

items.title: Austin trip day two: I ask to pay with bitcoin and someone tried to choke me
items.text:
Hey stackers,

Writing from the poker room after a four hour session. Taking a long break before I head back. Here’s my favorite hand from the sesh if you’re interested:

https://stacker.news/items/1603097/r/SatAttack?commentId=1603670

I woke up later than I wanted to knocking on my hotel door. It was 930 and housekeeping wanted to clean my room. I politely declined, got out of bed, brushed my teeth and quickly made my way out. There were things to see and bitcoin to spend. @plebpoet had recommended Caffe Medici as a place you can buy coffee and pastries for sats so that’s where I went first. There’s three locations and with some poking around I found the origional one. It’s in a nice quiet part of town and the ambience from outside looked really cool.

Here’s their BTCmap: [https://btcmap.org/merchant/way:382559089](https://btcmap.org/merchant/way:382559089)

![](https://m.stacker.news/163624)

![](https://m.stacker.news/163625)

I loved these stone chairs and tables. I wish I could have captured them all but some were being used and I didn’t want to take pictures of strangers. Inside was really nice too. Lots of plants and plenty of seating. I head to the counter where I see their square terminal and order a red eye which if you don’t know is an espresso shot with a regular coffee poured over it. It will clear the mind and wake up the bowels. Good for the morning. Right in the middle of asking if she would accept bitcoin she rings me up and answers my question; I see that wonderful toggle in the top left of some square terminals. I toggle to Bitcoin and I’m presented with a lightning address. I pay it with Phoenix no issues.

I asked her how often people pay with bitcoin—not very often, I guessed. She said only some times. She had been working there for four months and I was the third person to pay with sats. Not bad actually, I thought. It’s not like she rings everyone up, so there could have been others.

After a few sips of coffee and a couple pages from the second book of the Outlander series by Diana Gabaldon, I realized I had forgotten to check the parties! Fool boy. I asked where they came from, I don’t remember the name, but they get them from a local bakery here in Austin. I ended up with a blueberry muffin and toggled over to Bitcoin and sent another successful transaction.

![](https://m.stacker.news/163627)

![](https://m.stacker.news/163628)

I had plans to go to jiujitsu at the Austin 10th planet at 11 but waking up late was really deterring me from executing that plan. I really wanted to skip the workout and stay on this couch with my book and coffee. I read and read some more and checked the time. It was 1030. The gym was only 15 min away. There was time to not skip…. Over to my left I notice they have whole beans for sale on the shelf and decide there. I’ll
Buy some beans and stop being lazy. After the third lightning transaction in the last hour she tells me you get a free coffee with a bag of beans purchase….. UuuUgh it really sounded nice to sit and read with my free cup. Instead I take it to go and head to the gym.

![](https://m.stacker.news/163629)

I arrive at the gym 10 minutes before class time. I didnt bring a rash guard so I needed to buy one and told the guy over the counter as much. I asked if I could pay for both with bitcoin and he was a bit hesitant. “I think so” he said. He’s showing me the options for rash guards that are hanging on the racks when I see a box on the floor with some orange and black material inside. The box is labeled “b-coin”

Are these rash guards?! I ask
Oh yeah, they are. You want one of those?
Uuuuh YEAH. He pulls one out and shows it to me and it’s AWESOME. Here it is on me:

![](https://m.stacker.news/163630)

He had to text the owner and inquire about my bitcoin request. She responded pretty quickly and texted him a QR code made by cash app. The ones that you can pay either lightning or on-chain to. I took the opportunity to save some liquidity from my Phoenix channel and paid on-chain with Blue Wallet. I told him he should let her know I made an on-chain payment and that I was confident she’d be ok with that. And that she should receive the payment in about ten minutes. I paid 3sats/vB to ensure that was accurate.

Equipped with my new sweet rash guard it was time to start class. Everyone was very welcoming in introductions and we got to work pretty quickly. We warmed up with some bridges and shrimps and got right into the lesson. Today we were going to work on getting a hip toss from full guard and failing the attempt some attacks you can do instead.

My partner was great, I wish I remembered his name. I’m fairly novice, and he was patient and helped me with some important details on the attacks we were learning. We went over locking the Americana after the failed hip toss, then the guillotine, the triangle, the kimura, and omaplata all stemming from the original hip sweep attempt from full guard. during practice  I took a nasty elbow to the lip that swelled right away and filled my mouth with an iron taste (wear a mouthguard kids). Lesson complete, the next hour was open mat. They started the 5 min repeat clock and let people get sparring rounds in. I did a couple before hit hitting the showers. I’m a bit out of jiujitsu shape haha. Awesome stuff. Awesome class. Thanks coach Curtis!

![](https://m.stacker.news/163631)

On my way out the gym coach Curtis was at the front desk. I had asked him earlier for this group picture and told him I will
Blog about my day today on a forum. “Blog or vlog?” He asked.

Blog.

“People still read?” Haha YES I told him. And I told him where I’d blog as well I told him about stacker news and what it’s like. I told him the idea that because valuable things are used to express like-ness valuable content surfaces to the top. I showed him my stacker news and made a couple zaps. He was really intrigued. “A negligible amount I assume, like a small amount of sats?” Ummmm YES SIR. I was happy to hear him use the word sats. Bitcoin was normal for him, it seemed. He said he will check it out and that seemed like the perfect opportunity to give him one of the SN stickers @k00b gave me yesterday. items.title: The Origins of the Y Combinator
items.text:
Ha, you thought this was going to be about *Y Combinator*, the famous startup accelerator, didn't you?  Well, I tricked you, this post is actually gonna be about math.  (But don't worry, at the end it is loosely related to the business).

The "Y Combinator" is a term originating from *lambda calculus*, which, roughly speaking is the "language" mathematicians use to talk about functions.   The term originates from Haskell Curry, though similar ideas were already in circulation by the time he popularized it.

The Y Combinator is a **function that finds the fixed point of any other function**.  That is, the Y combinator is defined with the following relation:

$$YF = F(YF)$$

In words, "Y applied to F" is the same as "F applied to (Y applied to F)".

Why is this useful?  Without getting in to too much detail, it is what allows the lambda notation to describe functions that refer to themselves.  In other words, it allows for *recursive functions*, which can be quite useful in computation.

It can also be used to generate a lot of [paradoxes](https://stacker.news/items/1585258), because it is what lets a function reference itself, and many paradoxes arise from self referentiality.  In fact, Curry called his Y Combinator the "paradoxical combinator".

This self-referential property is what inspired Paul Graham, founder of Y Combinator the startup accelerator, to choose its name.  From the Y Combinator [FAQ](https://www.ycombinator.com/faq):

> Q: Why did you choose the name Y Combinator?
>
> A: The Y combinator is one of the coolest ideas in computer science. It's also a metaphor for what we do. It's a program that runs programs; we're a company that helps start companies.

To be mildly pedantic, the Y Combinator isn't just a program that runs other programs.  It's actually a program that allows *another* program to *run itself*.  In a way, that's even a better description, because an accelerator is a company that helps other companies become self sustaining.

Pretty cool history huh?  Hope this helps you sound smart at parties.

***

Economist bonus:  Fixed points are vitally important in economics.  Not just economics, but any dynamical system.  In fact, every equilibrium is actually a fixed point.

Imagine that $$F$$ describes a rule to transform the state of the world from the current state to the next state, i.e.:

$$X_{t+1} = F X_t$$

The world is in equilibrium if $$X$$ is a fixed point of $$F$$.  That is, if:

$$ X = F X $$

This means that $$X$$ is a world state that stays fixed even after the transformation is applied.

And guess what?  $$ Y F $$ is the fixed point of $$F$$.  So the Y-Combinator by definition lets us find the stable point of any dynamical system.  Or a market equilibrium in economics.

Cool stuff.

items.title: 🌳 Permaculture - American Chestnut a Keystone and my Discovery
items.text:
# Wild Chestnut: a gift of natural capital at the homestead

The American chestnut was a keystone species of the woods but it is effectively extinct after the Chinese chestnut blight ravaged the population over a hundred years ago. Cryphonectria parasitica (chestnut blight). The American chestnut has a fast growing timber form, abundant and consistent nut production, and the combination of the easily decomposing leaves and nurturing canopy creates habitat, sustenance, and fertility for not just wildlife but also for the people of eastern North America.

![](https://i.nostr.build/Wl9KHQK0dCA5jMcNaKa7is.jpg)
*(An extreme example of how large American chestnut trees were in the late 1800s)*

**A Rare Discovery at the homestead**
Here at the homestead, about 7 years ago, I discovered a lucky survivor of the blight. This chestnut tree is mature, producing nuts, and continues to grow!

![](https://i.nostr.build/K3C2BDIPp0Y0h0kSINa7rI.jpg)
![](https://i.nostr.build/TzYgz82XBw63Mh6Gx0aibi.jpg)
The chestnut tree discovery occoured shortly after having some logging done to promote the growth of the sugar maple trees here at the homestead. The pathways the loggers left behind allowed me to easily put up fencing in the woods, which meant I could now keep my horses and rams off the pasture, leaving all the grass growing at the homestead available for feeding ewes and lambs for meat. One day, while doing some work in the woods in the new horse paddock, I found the distinctive chestnut hull and upon further search, some nuts!

![](https://i.nostr.build/9lwn4zPsdGZsY6e3.jpg)
Upon first finding the hills, I thought to myself, where the heck did these come from? A chestnut tree! Where the heck is the chestnut tree? I was looking around horizontally, and saw nothing. Then I looked up to find the chestnut tree towering over me. I spent several more days looking for additional nuts but I must have just gotten lucky with the first few I found. The squirrels beat me to the rest of them. After finding the tree, I quickly came to the realization that if this tree is producing nuts then maybe there are younger trees to found nearby, the offspring.

![](https://i.nostr.build/1z7yRD0CCiEaqszXEwjFxx.jpg)
![](https://i.nostr.build/Royn.jpg)
Sure enough there were! I found a couple young seedlings within 50ft of the tree. One died because it was within the ram paddock and I couldn't protect it from the rams. Eventually they ate it. The second tree, I have been taking care of for several years. It has been nibbled at by the horses and sheep several times but continues to grow. I have yet to eat one chestnut from the large mature chestnut tree, so far I have been trying to sprout them and grow more trees. 

![](https://i.nostr.build/6DFAF1spoHABfbpmzKCVMw.jpg)
Just one year before discovering the wild Chestnut, I choose to plant some hybrid chestnuts I started from seed in the exact area where the mature tree is. I chose that location based on what I read were the ideal growing conditions for chestnut. Sandy light soil. Finding the wild Chestnut tree was confirmation that I had chose the location for the chestnut plantation well!

![](https://i.nostr.build/GX6MVFV6AXmXlyl1Vxmeac.jpg)

While this tree is unlikely a true American chestnut, it's probably some kind of American/European hybrid, the tree has many of the characteristics that made the American chestnut the keystone species that it was. Finding a wild Chestnut tree like this is incredibly rare and a sign to me that I've chose the right place to put down roots and prove to myself that permaculture will lead to a abundant and resilient lifestyle.

items.title: All Ownership is Provisional: Can You Own a Forest? What About a Bitcoin?
items.text:
[*The Natural Dividend*](https://link.amazon/B01NaCYkn) is getting ridiculous now.

I started this project on the recommendation of an [in-depth long read](https://blog.landeconomics.org/p/book-review-the-natural-dividend) about how to think *properly* about nature (https://stacker.news/items/1521292): commodity, property, usage. Basically, a philosophical assessment and discussion around the main economic topics that matter -- scarcity, efficiency, who gets what and why etc etc, how do we coexist and *peacefully cooperate* when we want to use specific things for competing ends.

At first, I found the academic, lefty nature-worshipping lunacy bearable: not nice, not ideal, but the intellectual price I had to pay for admission. 

## 38 pages in, I'm about to tear the pages off their bindings

These (left-wing!) academics are retarded. 

It's getting pretty disgusting. In fact, [given the pair of books](https://stacker.news/items/1587500) by Ben de Waal, a "libertarian" socialist Bitcoiner (yeah, try that one... if you thought *progressive* Bitcoiner was one hell of a contradiction, welcome to this madness), that I embarked on, it's highly relevant. Also, speaking of the monstrosity that is *progressivism* in general:

...**I genuinely think that leftwing-climate-conscious academics have lower cognitive capacities** than the rest of us. Their heads are just not screwed on right -- pun, very much intended. It takes a special amount of PhD lunacy to believe certain things.

On a more serious note: as leftist ideas have **dominated** politics and academia and media for the better part of a century, those of us with a freer persuasion have engaged with and understood the leftist case much better and much deeper than the academic insiders ever have/ever could appreciate e.g., a conservative or libertarian worldview. The asymmetry is painful… even [Jonathan Haidt’s moral foundations framework](https://www.facebook.com/jonathanhaidt/photos/my-colleagues-and-i-revised-moral-foundations-theory-to-do-a-better-job-of-expla/2079950535564617/) [results](https://yukaichou.com/behavioral-analysis/moral-foundations-theory-haidt-care-fairness-loyalty/) are pretty clear on this: conservatives can “speak” more moral languages than progressives can, progressives who are, quite *literally*, less empathetic in the strict meaning of the word. 

Fuck the boomers. Fuck the left. And fuck the academics.

***

## OK, back to business: Can You Own a Forest?

Jonathon Moses and Anne Margrethe Brigham started this [(same!) chapter](https://stacker.news/items/1565551) with a cool, provocative, absurd question about owning the sun. Of course **nobody does (or can) own the sun**, or block anybody else from accessing sunlight (When I mentioned this to Ben in Helsinki, he snarled something like "just wait for it!" or "with enough tech, they will!" again betraying a complete understanding of capital conditions and economic scarcity... **it's not tech or law**, it's E-C-O-N-O-M-I-C-S.)

...

![](https://m.stacker.news/160211)

Of course you can *own a forest*, in precisely the same way you can own a chainsaw.

I have greater **possession** over the chainsaw, seeing as how it's in my basement (which I may or may not, according to these authors' twisted logic, own), and it's smaller in size, so I can physically move it, *possess it* in a way I can't a forest (=doesn't fit in my hand, doesn't have a handle). The forest, however, is out *there* and -- if the stackers will allow the pun -- *rooted in place*. But what do any of those things have to do with ownership?

Ownership (=property) is a social relationship about who gets to do what. More to the point, it's the amount of violence someone exerts on you if you break that ownership bond... steal my chainsaw, let's say; burn down my forest. 

The authors cite Honoré (1961) from an Oxford jurisprudence essay on the 11(!) *incidents* of property but it all comes down to the one single, social-cooperation and social-harmony (shout-out HHH) aspect: **who decides what a good, asset, or thing does when there are rival, mutually exclusive claims/wishes on it?** 
Your car isn't used for the majority of the day/week... what's the reason, economically or philosophically, that [someone else can't "borrow](https://mises.org/free-market/case-hoarding)" it in the meantime? Some worthy cause like a homeless guy napping in there to avoid the rain, let's say. 

Economically speaking, ownership is optionality. Basically: rivalrousness and excludability rule everything. (Which, if you've ever delved down the economic rabbit hole of the social calculation debate as I have, is *the* [components on which everything turn](https://www.mercatus.org/hayekprogram/research/books/rivalry-and-central-planning).)

## Ownership is, like the authors partially outline in this section, the right or first-lien decision on how the item/good/resource is and can be used.

> What we think of as 'private property' in nature is really an abstract bundle of rights that governments grant to individuals or communities. (pp. 36-37)

Ah yes, just how the government owns your house and a government can rescind/take/expropriate any of your stuff at any point.

The fact that they are restricted from doing this by a legal system concerned with whose property is used by whom is SORT OF the definition of a legal order: *rule of law, individual liberty* etc etc. If none of those words have meaning, and the *default* mode of ownership is 100% ruled by the government (who, I'm convinced the authors say while suppressing a laughter, *represent you, the people*), there is no legal order: only (military) might makes right. If so: ***what in the world are we doing here?!***

Look, the fact that a government can rescind or override property claims — practically, physically, militarily, or even "legally" — doesn't invalidate that ownership or property exists (dare I say *precede?!*) irrespective of a government. It doesn't therefore follow that *no* property claims are real; that all ownership is provisional or resort/revert to a government if and when it so chooses.

Or, if you wanna go to that insanity: **Bitcoin.**

By this insane theory (that government owns everything, and it just *lets* you pretend that what is yours is temporarily yours), *nothing* is owned by anybody ever. Oh, but that UTXO somehow refuses to move; you can "own" it all you want, hashtag [New York Finder's Keepers example](https://stacker.news/items/1498602), but it changes nothing about the world. If I hold the private key to a UTXO that you "own" I can move it nonetheless; tell you to royally fuck off in the OP\_RETURN.

As always, Bitcoin stands unique here. Being a commodity without physical dimensions — [element zero, in Knut Svanholm’s phrasing](https://mises.org/mises-wire/sebag-and-natural-money) — it is the first and only thing you can truly own. Not own in a *legal* sense, because Bitcoin, the blockchain, doesn’t care what your laws say: You may have *legal title* to some UTXO, but it matters not.

In fact, and Stephen Kinsella said this directly and uncompromisingly [on stage in Helsinki, too](https://stacker.news/items/1585380): Bitcoin, being *pure information*, cannot be owned. It’s technically and praxeologically speaking just secret information, available and open to all, just accessible to almost nobody.

All you have when you have a UTXO is a highly probabilistic *asymmetric* ability to move funds. Baseline, everyone has some (exceedingly low) probability to spend a given UTXO. You, holding the private key or the seed phrase backup, have a much larger probability — prob-***ability*** — to spend. The entire legalistic edifice of rights goes out the window: it’s *all* ability; possession becoming [ten-tenths of the law.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Possession_is_nine-tenths_of_the_law)

For analogy, my chess brain went to Magnus Carlsen. He has no “right” to win every chess game against chess low-lifes like me; if we were pitted against each other for a trophy, the victory isn’t his *by right*. It’s his by ability: through his superior (asymmetric) information and skill, he will win every time. Just like *your* UTXO is secured by *your* superior ability to move it relative to mine.

***

And when the moronic morons couldn't get worse... *they found a lower low*:

![](https://m.stacker.news/160212)

## Why would (3) be the "default setting," you absolute twatheads?

Or in meme form: **when did** [**this become the default**](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ch5_j2q8ZPI)**?!**

If all you wanted to do and say with this book was, *All Your Stuff Are Belong To Us*, then why the hell dress it up like this? How in the world could anybody, for more than a fleeting moment, consider that the *default* ownership position of everything is *the government*?! Plain-old theft and power grabs, masquerading as political philosophy and under the cover of academic intellectualizing.

Fuck.
Right.
Off.

***

Serious retort: I might as well say that (4) — or (1) — is the default setting, and that every government action to restrict, regulate, tax, or otherwise impose on this immaculate conception is in violation of rights and reason.

And stop with this passive-tense hidden-actor nonsense ("...is assigned"): no sex is "assigned" at birth; no income is "distributed" (h/t Rothbard) separately from production; and property rights to goods that are yours are not "assigned" by some prior tribunal, deciding the starting blocks for everyone else.

> As nature belongs to us in common, our representatives in government authorize this private 'taking'. They do this to keep the peace and protect the resources (from either inefficient or over-exploitation), for the benefit of the community they represent. (p. 37)

oh lord. *Please grant me the serenity to accept the things I cannot change (=other people's moronic ideas and their pathetically limited intellectual stature), and the strength to resist committing the vile damage I wish to inflict upon these fuckheads, ... and perhaps the wisdom to know to which books to direct my attention.*

*TL;DR*: **left-wing people are not impressive; academics are full of it/themselves; this book is the trashiest nonsense bullshit intellectual nonsense I've ever had the misfortune to stumble across (...with the possible exception of the *Capitalism* book.** https://stacker.news/items/1561710**,** https://stacker.news/items/1562148**)**

items.text:
Hey stackers,

I write from the airport terminal in route to the chilly easy coast. What an incredible trip this has been. I’m normally looking forward to getting back home and returning to the recurrence of every day life. Not this time. I am not ready to leave and I know I’ll be back. Perhaps to live one day.

Yesterday morning I woke up at 3 AM a little hung over from all my wine at III forks and I couldn’t sleep. So I went to play poker. Got there at 4 AM and the crowd was wild. Everyone had been there since the night before and everyone seemed drunk, tired, or both. I played this huge hand and ended up winning a $1400 pot. https://stacker.news/items/1606387/r/SatAttack?commentId=1606424

I played until about 7 AM and headed out for breakfast. I ended up at a really nice diner called Phoebes diner and had a great meal. Forgot take pictures though. They sell slab bacon and serve it in thick deep fried slices. Wonderful. I get back to the hotel and sleep from 830AM to 12PM. @grayruby had recommended I take the 30 minute drive to visit lake Travis. After poking around on my phone for things around there I found a hike and a restaurant I wanted to do.

Here’s the all trail for the hike: [river place nature trail](https://www.alltrails.com/trail/us/texas/river-place-canyon-trail?sh=true)

The hike ended up being a great success. The weather was great and it was just the right amount of challenging to get the heart pumping.

![](https://m.stacker.news/164323)

![](https://m.stacker.news/164324)

I’ll take a little time to plug the Earth Runners here. For all my barefoot maxis out there this is a wonderful footwear for rocky environments where bare feet may have a tough time. I have taken these everywhere in all sorts of terrain. Love them.

Awesome hike. I was pleased to find good water flow and was surprised how clear it was! That tree going across the path is called the noggin knocker and there was a sign warning you not to knock your noggin haha.

Finishing my hike I was very ready for food and water and headed out to a restaurant right on Lake Travis called The Oasis. I didn’t really know what I was getting myself into but this place was GRAND. It’s a massive four story restaurant that’s the size of a big hotel. All four stories have a balcony that over looks the lake. There’s awesome art and decorations everywhere.

![](https://m.stacker.news/164331)

![](https://m.stacker.news/164332)

![](https://m.stacker.news/164333)

![](https://m.stacker.news/164334)

![](https://m.stacker.news/164335)

On my way in there was this blue metal UFO thing covered in stickers. I took the opportunity to put one of the stickers @k00b gave me on there. Turned out nice I think.

![](https://m.stacker.news/164336)

![](https://m.stacker.news/164337)

The food was decent. I got the chips and salsa. (Great chips!!) the chicken enchiladas with rice and beans, and a margarita on the rocks. I wasn’t planning on drinking but… the view made me.

![](https://m.stacker.news/164338)

![](https://m.stacker.news/164339)

I got back to my hotel around 6 pm and slept until 830. I had been deliberating between going to play poker one last time or going to find one last place to spend some sats. The issue was they were in opposite directions and I was really torn for a while. With one last check of BTCmaps I found a great solution. A place called Rockin Rolls that wasn’t in the downtown areas! It was close enough to the hotel and poker room to do both. So off I went. Here’s the BTCmap link [https://btcmap.org/merchant/node:13309320506](https://btcmap.org/merchant/node:13309320506)
It’s a small food truck in small gathering of food trucks right off the road. I appreciated the abundance of parking here!

![](https://m.stacker.news/164342)

![](https://m.stacker.news/164343)

These guys are awesome and if you’re a pizza eater in Austin I recommend giving this one a try. They make sourdough pizza rolls and they are very good. I ordered three classics (pepperoni and cheese) and a mini cannoli. Now time to pay. I see they only have the small white square terminal and I won’t be presented with the toggle option so I tell the man I’d like to pay with bitcoin if I can… he isn’t sure and calls the owner over who was thankfully there. He says “I think I set that up …” and we collectively poke around the terminal. Doesn’t take us long to find Bitcoin listed as one of the payment options and I tell them all we have to do is click that and it should generate me a QR code. It did and I made another seemless Phoenix payment. I gave my small spiel about how cool this is and how anyone who knows how can interact with this terminal with a bunch of different options.

The owner, Jake, was impressed and pleased. He was excited to see bitcoin being used and told me I was the first to do it. But on BTCmaps someone had verified the location in November 2025 so I was thinking perhaps not. I showed him BTCmaps and his little page on there and he thought that was very cool too! I told him that I would be blogging about this day and experience on stacker news and gave him the lowdown about what goes on here. “That sounds right my ally” he said. He loves community and according to him he likes crypto. He’s an ethereum guy he says. I told him I don’t know anything about it because I haven’t been able to move past Bitcoin. I was explaining what SN was and he understood immediately. “So instead of a like you just send over a little satoshi?” YEAH! I gave him a SN sticker and told him how to find us and that if he ever had any questions or inquires about using bitcoin in his business or other wise this is the place to come. I told him he would be very welcomed as a business owner accepting sats.

When I got my order I realized I didn’t have a drink. I asked for a bottle of water and had opened my Phoenix wallet to pay but he just said don’t worry about it. Thanks Jake!

I’ll say again, if you like pizza, come try this place. It’s awesome and he was telling me he’s looking to move to another state. Him and his wife love Austin but they’ve been there for 20 years and are ready for change. So time is running out!

![](https://m.stacker.news/164347)

After my pizza rolls it was time for one last poker sesh. I headed back to the lodge card club and played an uneventful 1.5 hours and won $10. I got gas for  the Turo rental, got to my hotel around 1130, and packed up. I had to be up at 530 to head to the airport.

I enjoyed my time in Austin very much and I really enjoyed sharing my experience here on stackers!! I’ve gotten a lot of support and a lot of engagement and that has been sweet. Thanks for reading and thank you to those who gave me awesome suggestions. I tried to do them all.

Whether you took up the challenge or not, there may be something for you in the following post. I have made an effort to give some original thoughts, followed by a character list and book summaries. As mentioned before, I am reading a hard copy of the translation of W.H.D. Rouse, but I can also recommend the* [*digitized version of the translation of A.S. Kline.*](https://www.poetryintranslation.com/PITBR/Greek/Odhome.php)

***

# leading themes and ideas

* post-war society leads to excess and decay
* culture, values, family, country -- all need to be defended by their inheritors
* the most commonly held belief is not always the correct one

# Commentary

The first three books show how Telemachos has been living and responding to the apparent death of his father, Odysseus. Unbeknownst to Telemachos, his father is lost at sea, dealing with cyclops, and upsetting Poseidon in the meantime. With the help of other greek heroes (Achilles, Agememnon, Nestor, Menelaus etc.), Odysseus led the Achaeans to victory at the battle of Troy, and since then, things have not been going so well back home. This is the setup for the poem.

This is a story of what happens in the aftermath of war, when a great society produces heroes that defend its culture and norms against outsiders, and how, despite their victory on the battlefield, this same culture must be defended in their absence. This is seen at the outset, when the gods discuss what has become of the house of Atreus, whose son, Agememnon, finds himself the victim of Agisthos. The latter is eventually murdered by Agememnon's own son, Orestes, in an act of revenge for the murder of his father and the destruction of his household. Zeus laments the fact that, although they have brought this terrible fate upon themselves, men continue to hold Zeus to account. Wherever the fault lay, the poem tries to reckon with the phenomenon where society grows weak in the absence of the warriors who will defend their culture.

As the drama of the poem ensues, it is revealed how political infighting led the Achaeans to split up after Troy, leaving Agememnon and Odysseus away from their homeland. In the latter's absence, his wife Penelope and his son Telemachos have been left to defend what is left of his household. Suitors consume Odysseus' wealth, as they loiter, courting Penelope.

**So far, I have taken the following from the poem, summarized in a few sentences:**

* A great culture, such as the Greeks had, will produce great warriors, in whose absence its greatness will quickly fall to shambles.
* There will always be those willing to feast on the spoils bought by the sweat and blood of another person's brow
* Even when an entire population believe one thing, it may not be true. Truth is not easily discerned, but found out through persistence, struggle and adventure.

So, to you, reader of Epic poetry, I ask the question:

* Where do you see yourself on this cycle (i.e. good times --> weak men --> bad times --> strong men?)
* Is there an analogue in modern culture to the suitors feasting on Odysseus' wealth?

***

# Reading notes:

key characters

* Odysseys: a great warrior from Ithica. Never returned from the battle of Troy, in which he earned his stripes as a hero.
* Telemachos: the son of Odysseus.
* Penelope: the wife of Odysseus. Awaiting Odysseus' return.
* Suitors: men gathered in Ithica, enjoyers of Odysseus' house and belongings, as they vie for Penelope's hand in marriage.
* Zeus: Father of the gods. Feels let down by mortal men because of what happened in the aftermath of the battle of Troy concerning Agememnon.
* Aigisthos: killed Agememnon and married his wife. Is then killed by the latter's son, Orestes.
* Agememnon: in the aftermath of the battle of Troy, did not wish to sail home, for fear of displeasing Athena. He splits from Diomedes and Nestor, and stays in Troy
* Athena: Zeus' daughter. Favors Odysseus, intervenes for him so as not to see his house come into ruin
* Poseidon: god of the seas
* Mentes/Mentor: Athena in the form of a man, advises Telemachos in Ithica and in Pylos.
* Aigyptios: Wise councilman, blesses Telemachos
* Nestor: son of Neleus, king of Pylos.

# Book Summaries:

## Book I

> These men amuse themselves with music and song, freely, since they consume another’s wealth without repayment, one whose white bones are tumbling in the waves, or rotting in the rain on some far shore
> \--Mentes.

Zeus and Athena meet on Olympus. Lament Agememnon's murder and betrayal by Aigisthos. Athena descends from Olympus to intervene into the affairs of Telemachos, to keep him from a similar fate. His father, Odysseus, suffers the ire of Poseidon, who keeps him from returning home against the will of the other gods. Suitors, who think Odysseus is dead, harass Penelope and Telemachos, and take advantage of the latter's good manners. No one really knows whether Odysseus has died. Telemachos answers Mentes that he does not stop the suitors from courting his mother for the dread of not knowing what has come of his father. Before transforming into a bird to depart, Athena rouses Telemachos to gather the lords together and order them to stop, and moreover, that he should go out in search of his father.

## Book II

> ‘My lords, my Suitors, though Odysseus is dead and you are eager for me to marry, have patience till I complete this work, I do not want it wasted, this shroud for noble Laertes, ready for when pitiless death’s cruel end overtakes him: since I fear some Achaean woman of this land would blame me, if he who won great wealth lay there without a shroud.’
> \--Penelope

Telemachos assembles the lords of Ithica and makes his case, demanding that and end be put to the suitors' behavior. Antinous rebukes him, saying that Penelope has tricked them for the past three years, by saying she would choose a husband when the finishes weaving the shroud of Odysseus' father, Laertes, which she would work on during the day only to unravel the work she had completed under the darkness of night. Zeus sends an omen portending the destruction of the suitors. Athena again urges Telemachos to go in search of his father, provisions a ship and a crew for him, and even afflicts the suitors in Telemachos' home with drowsiness. Telemachos sets sail for Pylos in search of news of his father.

## Book III

Telemachos arrives at Pylos, where the people all pay sacrifice to the gods. Telemachos and Mentor make an offering to Poseidon, in Nestor's name. Telemachos appeals to Nestor, who also fought at Troy, to give news of what happened to Odysseus. He reports that the latter was caught in the middle of a feud between Menelaus, who wished to depart after the battle of Troy, and Agememnon, who feared the angering the gods, and wished to wait. Nestor and Odysseus went with Menelaus, leaving Agememnon behind. In a moment of hesitation, however, Odysseus turned back to join Agememnon. Nestor and Menelaus sail from Troy together and in the meantime, Aigisthos overtakes Agememnon, killing him and taking his wife for marriage. Nestor urges Telemachos to look on the heroism of Orestes, who took revenge against and murdered his father's murderer, Aigisthos. He tells Telemachos he needs to visit Menelaus for news of what came of Odysseus. Nestor offers Telemachos his men and ships, his hospitality, they sacrifice a heifer to Athena, and set off at dawn.

Hi there,

We built Bitcoin Arena: games and prediction markets on Bitcoin. It is fully decentralized. There is no company running the rounds, no central server and no custodian. Anyone can run a node, and anyone can offer an app. It’s live on testnet4, and we need people outside the team to try both.

There’s no token and nothing to buy. Test sats are free and have no value.

Anyone can run a node

* Install it on Windows, macOS or Linux. A setup window walks you through it.
* Post a bond on Bitcoin and take a seat.
* Host apps, verify rounds and earn a share of the fees.
* No permission needed. Your bond is your ticket in.

Anyone can offer an app

* Write your game and sign it, and any node can host it.
* The nodes replay every round with your rules.
* There’s no approval and no listing fee.
* You earn 2% of every paid round in your app.

How a round stays honest

* A Bitcoin block hash draws the committee of nodes, so nobody picks who decides.
* Stakes lock in a Fedimint federation run by the nodes.
* A result counts only when 5 of 7 nodes confirm the same one, and anyone can object for 10 minutes.

How you can help

* Run a node on testnet4 and tell us where setup was hard.
* Build a small app and tell us what’s missing in the docs.
* Play Tick Tock Next Block, Rock Paper Scissors or the 15-minute Bitcoin Up or Down market and try to break it.
