items.text:
**Here's an interesting (but dated) one... from the amazing Substack "Net Interest."**

I had occasion today to look through point and reward economics, and next to central banking or sex trafficking or whatever it must be one of the most despicable industries out there. It's well-known that loyalty cards/rewards schemes are fiat money-printing scams that, at best, saddles the user with a below-mininum wage job (https://stacker.news/items/869415).

...but it's good for the companies running these schemes. (Yea, no shit: the money printing/issuing was always great, and under shitty monetary regime there's an incentive for everyone to become a bank or a bank-like entity #[743123](https://stacker.news/items/743123), https://stacker.news/items/1329539)

It's a typical example where businesses do things **against the interest of their customer** (thus, it's dishonest) *while looking* like they're providing you with extra benefits. Somebody should call Lizzy (Warren!). (Also, it's one area where the European Union, in its infinite overlording wisdom, made a limiting regulation that was *actually good* for us Europooreans! By capping interchange fees, they basically outlawed rewards programs and saved/spared 500 million Europeans the time/necessary effort to play these silly money games.)

***

In the age of card networks and (FX) spreads (https://stacker.news/items/1586158) and costs to merchants, the COST and BENEFITS of these (Ponzi?) schemes become entirely intransparent where everyone, like in democracy, think they might get one over on someone else.

At best, it's a selection-biased gamble where **sophisticated consumers take advantage by optimizing the terms/conditions/value of the whole scheme vs naive consumers** who mistakenly believe they can/will win, while the house (as every properly set-up gamble) wins. The naive consumers will inevitably make some sort of error in their financial behavior (overdrafts, not enough spending, not maximizing rewards, too small fish such that annual fee eats up all other benefits).

The most well-known examples here are

* **bank deposits**: people hold too much cash at low-yielding bank accounts vs what they could/optimally should keep in higher-yielding savings accounts. The difference, while maaaybe sometimes convenient for the customer, end up in aggregate securing a massive windfall (=cheap financing) for the banks
* **life insurance products**: life insurance is usually priced very affordably and attractively for the buyer, which the insurance company isn't doing out of ignorance or stupidity but because they know from experience that some portion of the buyers (accidents, life circumstances changing, or just neglect) will let their policies lapse after having paid for a few years, meaning free money for the company, or worse, sell it back to the company at a great discount (=again, free money)

Here's the conclusion from a Fed paper on the subject from a few years ago:

> regardless of income, sophisticated individuals profit from reward credit cards at the expense of naïve consumers. To probe the underlying mechanisms, we exploit bank-initiated account limit increases at the card level and show that reward cards induce more spending, leaving naïve consumers with higher unpaid balances \[...]
> Naïve consumers might underestimate these payments and incur costs from usage. Sophisticated consumers, in contrast, might rake in the benefits while avoiding the payments and thus profit from usage

Here's the graph they use to display the idea (sorted by FICO scores, but the same point stands)

![](https://m.stacker.news/162147)

*tl;dr*, the area between the curves is larger on the negative side than the positive side, thus a) redistributing from naive to sophisticated, but more importantly b) makes the entire scam profitable to the company to run: What it has to pay the sophisticated winners is less than what they manage to extract from the idiot losers.

## The entire edifice is a combination of beggar-thy-neighbor and race to the bottom, with misperception and money illusion becoming key features.

From our pal Matt Levine in a recent Money Stuff piece

> banks make a lot of their money from depositor inattention: When interest rates go up, bank customers mostly don’t move their money, because it would be a pain, so banks can pay below-market interest rates on their deposits.
> You could have similar worries about life insurance, or annuities, or mortgages: Lots of financial products are built (and priced) based on assumptions about customer inattention.

The strategy is that you intentionally misprice (underprice) your service, banking on the fact that, in aggregate, enough people who opt in for this juicy, nice-looking offers will make enough errors that the few sophisticated customers who take perfect, optimized advantage of the mispricing won't cost the company.

***

ANYWAY, **Marc Rubenstein walks through the logic and economics of loyalty programs** and points(!) to some of the intricate cross-subsidized and legal/economic oddities with these programs:

> A key question in the whole points dynamic is how much partners pay for miles. Avios Group deferred revenue at a rate of 0.88 pence per point on the stock it issued in 2023, its highest rate in many years. The consumer value of points varies widely according to how they are used, but The Points Guy puts the value of Avios at around 1.2 pence per point, so the benefit to the consumer is clear. 
> Because the airline can adjust the redemption rate to encourage the use of rewards in ways that reduce their marginal cost, it is able to offer rewards to card issuers at a discount.2 In this way, reward programs can generate profits for both issuers and airlines while generating loyalty to both, a significant positive sum outcome.

## “By minting points, airline companies are able to lock in substantial cash flows.”

> Online points-monitoring sites posting point “valuation” tables on a regular basis because of course the offers change and of course the issuer of this fake, unusable money manipulate it to their advantage.
> The only problem is that competition has been driving up the rate at which card companies pay rewards. Over the last 12 months, American Express has paid out 1.07% of purchase volume in rewards, up from 0.80% ten years ago. Other card issuers have seen similar reward inflation. Capital One paid out 1.29% of purchase volume in 2022, up from 0.80% in 2013. And Discover paid out 1.43%, up from 0.94%. 
> American Express was initially exempt from the EU rules, so my British Airways co-branded card remained unaffected. In 2018, though, the courts brought Amex into line. Fortunately, American Express agreed to eat the cost. My BA Premium Plus card continues to pay 1.5 Avios points for every £1 spent, equivalent to around 1.8% on the basis of The Points Guy’s 1.2 pence per Avios valuation. I guess I do pay £250 per year for the privilege, and Amex likely bought the points at a steep discount (in particular the batch they acquired in 2020 to help the airline out of a liquidity squeeze).

JUST that gives us a few intransparent economic flows:

* First: The Amex bailout of BA during ‘rona, purchasing made-up points at cheap discount… even if Amex nominally loses \~1.3% per dollar of EU transactions, if what they hand over to the customer in rewards (=made-up BA money) was acquired at well below par, there’s still a profit in it for the card company.
* Second, to recoup the yearly card fee of 250 quid, a user needs to transact just below £14,000 a year, basically most of the discretionary card spending for a normal (Europoorean) person… and that’s not giving you pounds back, but made-up BA money you must do some additional trixing (in their webshops, for air fares, for lounge access or extra luggage etc) to benefit from.

## “there are clear subsidies at play. Someone, somewhere is subsidizing my points habit – no longer the merchant, it is now other BA or Amex customers. Indeed, such subsidies are the most controversial aspect to the model.”

I don't quite understand what this percentage is referring to (a larger share of Amex revenues are going back to users than before...?) but it seems to suggest that there is some sort of competitive pressure to close this rent-seeking gap

items.title: Why Were Victorian Elites so Effective? (Works in Progress Magazine, Sam Hughes)
items.text:
## Amazing (long) read, highly recommend

I like Works in Progress. *A lot*. It's a serious outlet for long-form journalism, and it (usually!) features writers whose minds are oriented correctly toward the future. (its editor-in-chief lost his mind during 'rona, so I've stayed away from reading/subscribing or even attempting to contribute... *but I'm often very tempted*)

![](https://m.stacker.news/160670)

## What's the Key For Success?

Work hard, long hours, education, 5am, cold plunges, diversity, pay your politicians well to avoid corruption *blah-blah*?

No, no:

> The elites of Victorian Britain operated differently. Their schools and universities were not terribly academic and had very little STEM. As adults, **they got up late, drank a lot, and spent a remarkable share of their waking hours partying.** They loved feasting, sports, holidays, dancing, and dressing up. Contrary to their stodgy reputation, they were probably a lot of fun.

> the elites of nineteenth-century Britain were, by their own lights, extremely successful. For much of the century, Britain was the richest country on Earth. Its companies dominated global commerce, industry and finance.

## In Defence of Debauchery

![](https://m.stacker.news/160674)

* **SCHOOLING:** while strict (early age, regulated times, single-sex away from family, corporal punishment), the values the English Victorian elite cultivated at boarding school were remarkably progressive: loyalty, internationalism, studies of the arts -- Latin and Ancient Greek --

Amazing:

> There was **resistance to the teaching of science, not because Victorians were hostile to science** in principle, but because they thought it **irrelevant to the kind of moral and cultural formation** that a school for gentlemen was supposed to provide.
> (By contrast, girls were not usually taught classics, meaning that, rather surprisingly, affluent Victorian girls generally followed a more modern curriculum than their brothers.)

While not obviously successful, it cultivated valuable skills:

> ...The most that can be said for Victorians’ classical education is perhaps that, like schooling in any difficult subject, it trained students in self-discipline, memorization, and applying rules.

And *this* we could definitely learn from today:

> Under such circumstances, it is perhaps unsurprising that the share of time spent in the classroom was relatively modest. At Rugby School, weeks were divided into three ‘full days’, three ‘half days’, and Sunday. On a full day, students spent about five hours in the classroom, compared with maybe two hours on a half day.  \[AND, importantly:] They also tended to be shorter than those of contemporary elite schools in France, Germany, or Italy, where the curriculum was normally more academically rigorous.

## "Victorians thought extremely highly of sports, believing that they instilled team spirit and endurance, fostered mutual loyalty, channeled energy and competitiveness, and taught men how to win and lose graciously."

One Loretto School headmaster described the school's priorities: **1) character, 2) physique,** 3) intelligence, 4) manners, 5) information. First time *brawns > brains, eh*

* **UNIVERSITIES**: Not much studying, plenty of "teambuilding"

I found *this* observation interesting:

![](https://m.stacker.news/160677)

> Oxbridge tutors believed overwhelmingly that the purpose of an undergraduate degree was not training for work nor even preparation for academic research, but rather a general moral and intellectual formation that would fit students for any professional role they might later pursue.

also:

> Fellowships were opened up to laymen in the later decades of the century, but **Oxford and Cambridge did not become world-leading research institutions until they were transformed by German scholars fleeing Nazism in the 1930s.** The dominance of Oxbridge in British culture was unusual: these institutions educated a much larger share of the elite than was the case for any two institutions in any other country

Fuck, these peeps just had *great* lives. (In some respects, Oxford life these days is very similar!)

![](https://m.stacker.news/160679)

* **ADULTHOOD**: Busy-busy-fucking busy bee... but not in the way you think

## "One virtue that upper-class Victorian education signally failed to inculcate was early rising. Although Victorian schoolboys and university students got up fairly early for chapel, the day of an upper-class Victorian adult started late."

Fuck *yeah!* Den loves victory https://stacker.news/items/1590741

The great statesmen and prime ministers back then "breakfasted at 9 am" or hosted a "social breakfast starting at 10.30 am (claret was served), continuing till about noon." **A-M-A-Z-I-N-G**

Also, not that different from today (minus the frock)

> general, however, Britain’s elites were slow to suburbanize, and in 1914 most still lived in centrally located row houses and walked to work. Every day a great herd of frock-coated men emerged from Belgravia and Mayfair and poured through Covent Garden to their offices in Parliament, Whitehall, the Inns of Court, and the City.

If you've noticed the drinking *at every goddamn meal*, you're not alone. It's pretty disturbing, an entire nation run by high-functioning alcoholics.

> The Victorians loved drinking and drank a lot by modern standards. Men drank more than women, but women drank a good deal too: one conduct guide[noted that](https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/12426/pg12426-images.html)‘young ladies seldom drink more than three glasses of wine at dinner but married ladies, professional ladies, and those accustomed to society, and habits of affluence, will habitually take five or even six, whether in their own homes or at the tables of their friends’.

...and the partying, until the wee hours. Plus, for some odd reason Americans call this "Irish exit" (or French goodbye):

![](https://m.stacker.news/160682)

And they were hardly just for entertainment:

> the social events of the Victorian elite were notable for their lack of segregation by age or sex. A Society ball discharged the functions of both a teenage house party and a business networking convention: in fact, it*was* both a teenage house party and a business networking convention. \[...] Unmarried young people (and their unfortunate parents) might go to three or four balls per week, while other Society members would go to one or two. But the other nights were scarcely less busy. Opera, theatre and concerts were important, especially opening or gala nights.

Fuck, dudes kept busy.

> An MP might miss dinner for a late sitting of Parliament, but still drop into a soirée at 10.30pm, turn up to a supper party at 11.45pm, and then arrive at a ball at 1am. From February to July, the Victorian upper class led a remarkably nocturnal existence, with bedtimes in the small hours and the mornings something of a write-off.

## "All else being equal, rich and powerful Victorians must have been less productive for spending four hours a day in the office rather than twelve. But the creation of a single ruling *Gemeinschaft* may have had compensatory advantages."

Domestic and international (geo)political implications:

> This obviously had advantages for Britain. The elites of the American South had a very different identity to those of the North, and ultimately led the country into civil war. Spain, Italy and France suffered from incessant conflicts between urban bourgeois and rural nobility. Germany was riven with strife along geographical, religious, and class lines. **Some of these tensions existed in Britain, but except in Ireland, the elite finessed them peacefully.**

## "Would modern societies work better if their local and national government were conducted by a tight-knit community of extremely rich and successful people?"

items.title: In Search of Freedom: Life, Death, and Sovereignty in the Himalaya
items.text:
![](https://m.stacker.news/164458)

*I’m sitting in a dusty hotel room in Kathmandu, attempting to call a Spanish airline about my missing luggage.*
*“We’ll have to email our ground staff contractor,” they say.*
*I try to protest. “My trek starts tomorrow!”*
*“Please check your email later today, sir.”*
*I listen to the click of the agent hanging up the phone.*

The hotel is nestled precisely in the middle of Thamel, the tourist district with its colourful flags, rooftop gardens, and too-narrow streets. There is plenty to do in the capital, but after three days of chasing my lost bag in a Kafkaesque system of virtual shrugs and missed callbacks, my energy wanes. I am trapped in the antipresent, unable to visit any tourist attractions, only capable of reconnecting to the hotel WiFi to refresh my emails for the 800th time in the hope of news. With nothing but time, I feel utterly trapped.

During a 2018 volunteering trip to Nepal, I waited for my opportunity to walk the Annapurna Circuit: a two-week hiking route crossing high paths and winding through tiny Buddhist villages. Instead, I got a call to fly back to the UK. My father had been diagnosed with bowel cancer, and it was terminal. He was the one who introduced me to hiking, taught me to be patient when faced with another false peak, to understand the swirling patterns of clouds, to clean my kit, to be prepared for sudden change, to appreciate in the silence of the wilderness, to be present. Near the end, we talked a lot about hiking.

“When you see a mountain,” he said, “think of me.”
I can’t remember what I said in return.

It took eight years to get back to Nepal — grief, travel, COVID, relocation, work, money, rule changes, and procrastination saw to that. After all my posturing about being an advocate for freedom, living my life exactly how I wanted, my fear of closure held me back. I wouldn’t gain perspective until I’d seen those mountains again.

***

![](https://m.stacker.news/164459)

*Finally, after another two-day delay, I take the first steps of my 18-day trek. The Manang Valley bathes in bright sunlight. We pass apple orchards and fields of buckwheat as we climb to Lower Pisang, but after nearly a week stuck in the hotel, I feel like I could run up the path for hours. I’m not doing this alone; there are ten in my group — other travellers looking for answers in the hills. We get to know each other in the brief moments when we’re not gasping for breath in the thinning air.*

That night, I fire up my Kindle and read [*The Ones Who Walk Away From Omelas*](https://shsdavisapes.pbworks.com/f/Omelas.pdf). It’s one of my all-time favourites, a short story that’s more of a thought experiment. Ursula Le Guin presents a Utopian society of harmony, peace, and joy. In Omelas, life is wonderful for every resident except one: a miserable child, suffering alone in a dungeon. Most residents can ignore the one person whose incarceration guarantees their joy and freedom, but the few who can’t leave the citadel forever.

Maybe it’s hubris, but I’ve always considered myself one of those who ‘walk away’. I’ve been willing to give up convenience to claw back some of the sovereignty I’d lost through a corporate job and living in a mediocre London suburb. And here I was on a legendary remote hiking route, perhaps not scaling peaks, but at least challenging myself, climbing higher than I’ve ever been.

***

![](https://m.stacker.news/164462)

*The nights are cold at 4000m above sea level, and my wardrobe is more suited to the Spanish summer than sub-zero temperatures. As we hike farther up, across metal suspension bridges and past well-insulated herds of yaks, I wear my father’s old gear — a down vest and the bright red* *waterproof. It’s not a homage; it’s purely practical. Still, it gives me some kind of connection.*

I feel him silently judging me for walking the ‘tourist trail’. He always had to plan the route and bring every bit of kit himself, while a Nepalese porter carries my luggage strapped directly to their forehead. He would also have loved seeing the world’s highest peaks up close and listening to the guides' explanations of the dangers, the routes, the climbers. We all live the battle of comfort vs sovereignty.

The ‘tea house’ hotels in the Manang valley have a few more mod cons than expected. Some even have hot showers. But today, the power for the whole village is out. As the sun sets, my roommate and I read by the light of our headtorches.

Before the trip, I’d just finished reading *The Gulag Archipelago*, Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn’s brutal account of the anti-freedoms of Communist Russia. That night, I search for a quote that jumped off the page when I read it: ‘All those years in our cells and our huts, the state’s electricity had seared our souls, and now, darkness was bliss.’ Sometimes, our only freedom comes through stoic minimalism and absence. I turned off my reading light and listened to the darkness.

***

![](https://m.stacker.news/164463)

*I’m in bed with a worsening cold. The lack of doctors and pharmacies doesn’t seem so quaint when you are coughing up your lungs. The 5,416m Thorong La Pass plays on my mind, and I struggle to sleep. It’s not just me; another member of the group has a virus, and most of the others are blowing their runny noses in the dry mountain air. We take each day slowly, climbing 500m in altitude, and putting one foot in front of the other. There aren’t any other options: turning back involves walking too, and I don’t like going backwards.*

By this point, we’ve walked 80km or so. [Karl Bushby](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq8rz38jr50go) has just finished walking 50,000km after circumnavigating the globe by foot. I watched a video on his trip just before setting off on mine, and I was most impressed by the fact he had no desire to break records, no charity campaign, no press team. “Every fibre of my being,” he says, “every day, has been what I'm doing right now.”

Along the way, between icy paths and sneezes, I hit upon the idea that walking is trustless. That’s why it is so freeing to Karl Bushby and to all of us. You don’t rely on anyone or anything else. It is the rhythm of taking one step at a time. Sometimes things go as expected; sometimes they don't. But freedom is not about control. It depends on adapting to your surroundings and being in sync with the path. Each day, the tea houses serve another group of foreigners. Monks in the small temples perform another ceremony, another meditation. The kitchens produce another hundred plates of dal bhat, accompanied by ginger tea for the sniffling guests. The sun rises over snowy peaks again.

One of the guys in our group walked to Everest Base Camp more than 20 years ago. Things were quite primitive back then. He told me the soundtrack of those two weeks was the constant *thunk* of cattle bells. That was his rhythm, his surroundings. He bought a heavy metal bell in a Kathmandu market at the end of his trip and still displays it proudly in his New Jersey house.

***

![](https://m.stacker.news/164464)

*It’s 4 am and -15℃ on the day we climb over the pass and down the other side. Lines of headtorches light the steep path up, and the snow crunches under boots fitted with temporary metal spikes. The path ahead is backed up because a girl from another group has fainted. Her partner attempts to carry her up on piggyback, but stops after just a few steps.*

*As we wait for the last members of our party to arrive, we hop from foot to foot to keep warm. Frank, a German realtor who lives in Cape Town, excitedly tells us he has the WiFi password for a teahouse we’ve just passed. ‘Who cares?’ I think. ‘You’ve flown all the way here to cross this pass, and you’ve gotten up in the dark to do it. Why do you need WiFi?’*

Later, after the girl who collapsed has passed us riding on a yak, after we’ve taken our photos at the top, and after we’ve descended to 3,800 meters and bathed in the sun of the afternoon, I reflect on Frank and his need for WiFi passwords. Yes, we are all plugged into our digital worlds, but if you can’t spend a few hours away from it, are you really free at all?

I think about the amount of time I spent that day completely disconnected, staring at the contrast of birds of prey crossing white peaks and soaring up into a blue sky. Why do we struggle to think beyond the next unit of time? The next breath, photo, coffee break, the next day, the next WiFi access point. Why do we need to extract immediate value from our physical world?

I can’t always rein in my differences from the group. Not everyone has waited eight long years to reconnect with their father by climbing a Nepalese mountain. This is every fibre of my being, not just a social media photo op. My father would have loved to build a homestead, to fix machines, grow cattle, and walk the land, but he chose a secure life so his children could do that.

The next days we pass through small towns celebrating *Dashain* — a time for families, giving thanks, and taking stock. We stay with a local family and experience life in a small town; while we eat set meals and walk to a strict schedule, it feels like all the Nepalis around us are making their own choices.

We watch old ladies harvesting millet and corn. Heavy machinery continues to shift the earth of roads and riverbanks affected by landslides. We see new entrepreneurs opening restaurants, tea houses, and local stores. I speak to Ram, one of our guides, who is working through the festival period to put his kids through college in Japan. Everyone must hustle to improve their lot because saving in Rupees is futile. Even with remittances from those working abroad, Nepal is constantly playing catch-up. Everyone is building a better life here; no one expects it to be easy.

***

![](https://m.stacker.news/164466)

*My final day is spent in Kathmandu. A few of us travel to Durbar Square to see the world’s only living goddess. The Kumari is a young girl selected from a northern village. There are strict physical and mental tests as well as a birthdate that matches specific astrological criteria. She is taken from her parents to live in an opulent palace, where her feet may never touch the ground below. If she sheds a drop of blood, she is cast out into the realm of the mortals and is replaced by a new Kumari. Hindus and Buddhists alike come to see her, hoping to be blessed by one of her three daily appearances at her palace window. The current Kumari is just three years old. After waiting an hour for her to appear, I feel like her nervous little wave is an anticlimax. The crowd still gasps.*

Later, it hits me that she is the living embodiment of the child in *The Ones Who Walk Away from Omelas*. Instead of being tortured or in pain, she is doted on. She has expensive gowns, extravagant makeup, a team of handlers, tutors, and adoring fans, but she is cursed. Her childhood is stolen, and she is imprisoned to bring others luck, joy, and religious harmony. She cannot play, shout, hide, misbehave, cry, laugh, or neglect her duties. She cannot walk where she pleases. To tourists, the Kumari is a sweet anomaly, a curious tradition. To Nepalis, she is a living goddess. Almost everyone is happy with this arrangement.

![](https://m.stacker.news/164460)

I went to Nepal to reconnect with emotions I had long since buried. Curiously, I saw glimpses of freedom instead of apparitions of my father. Sometimes I saw them in the hawks cruising high above, sometimes in the industrious lives of locals, and sometimes in the restrictions of those trapped in digital worlds or religious constructs.

If there is one thing I learned on this journey across the Annapurna mountains, it is that freedom is gained one step at a time. You have to know which direction you are heading, and you must understand what you are leaving behind.

items.title: lichen: new layer 2 ledger idea - AdamISZ
items.text:
> **Lichen's idea** - some of [Bitcoin scripting] constraints are simply bypassed if you make one tradeoff: have the redemption be settled within a 2 party contract, whose outcome is adjudicated on Bitcoin, rather than have the actual contract be in Bitcoin directly.

I think Lichen looks a lot like the models we are used to with Ark and Spark or even a more streamlined version of single-channel lightning wallets like Phoenix and Lexe (the user deposits sats into a "hub" like an ASP or LSP). But if I understand it correctly, it reverses default outcomes so that it is the hub or sequencer's responsibility to stay make sure users don't cheat rather than the users responsibility to make sure the hub doesn't cheat. It relies on ZK proofs -- which seem to be the hope of every new L2.

> what happens if the hub just dies and disappears? Even worse if the sequencer dies too (which makes sense; here we're assuming they're the same entity). In this case you can't do more transactions on L2 because the sequencer that advances the L2 state is not responding. And you can't get the hub to agree to a withdrawal in your 2-of-2 contract either. But it's no problem; the contract has a clause "claim" that lets you post "here's the nullifier of my note and here's how much money it says I'm owed, and I can prove it". If the hub literally does nothing your claim stands, and after a timeout you can make that withdrawal (in fact such a hub is of course in danger of you posting an *invalid* proof to claim more than you're actually owed; but that's inevitable if it's dead and won't respond; it's not a failure of the protocol).
> 
> So, what if the hub is actually malicious? It stops processing L2; so you want to get out. You post the above "claim" but then it answers: to answer it has to do one of 2 things: (see detail in [the exit explainer](https://github.com/AdamISZ/lichen/blob/master/docs/explainers/exit.md)) either prove that your note is invalid because it was spent elsewhere --- that's a "counter-proof", or, prove that your ZKP of inclusion is invalid. We can enforce that who gets the money is the honest party, in every case. The only assumptions are the same ones you have in Lightning, but a bit stronger: you assume you can post transactions enforcing the adjudication successfully to Bitcoin's blockchain. 

Adam Gibson is pretty clear that the repo contains a lot of vibe-coded stuff, so I linked above to the one part that I believe he actually wrote. The following links, while explaining things more fully, have a lot of slop:

> *Want the full design* - read this short intro, then go to the main [design paper](https://github.com/AdamISZ/lichen/blob/master/papers/lichen-v0.4.1.pdf)
> 
> *Want to run the web demo* - that is, running the stack on regtest locally and playing with it in the browser to see how it operates: go [here](https://github.com/AdamISZ/lichen#the-demo).
> 
> *Want to understand the mechanics, in more detail than covered in the paper* - look at the growing set of [explainers](https://github.com/AdamISZ/lichen/blob/master/docs/explainers/README.md); these are AI generated and have lots of nice diagrams to take you through the steps of all the component parts. They vary from completely high level with no code/math to the guts of the dispute mechanism, the ZKP generation etc.

# #025 Feel the Breez

### Here comes everybody 🤖

Value transfer has a new kind of builder. Coding agents are bringing teams to bitcoin who’d never touched it before, and they’re putting it inside the products people use every day, all over the world. Here’s what happened in October at Breez:

* 🤖 *AI Is Eating Software*
* 💼 *Open for Business*
* ☕ *Coffee’s on Us*
* 🏦 *Lightning in the Wild: Bank On It*
* 🎙️ *Shoot the Breez Is Back*

***

## AI Is Eating Software 🤖

Fifteen years ago, Marc Andreessen wrote that software is eating the world. It has. Now AI is eating software, and AI and bitcoin are feeding each other’s rise.

We analyzed close to 1,000 integration requests going back to 2023, and since Claude Code arrived, new integration requests are up 14x. Requests from non-crypto apps are up 5x this year, and it’s accelerating: Q2 came in 61% above Q1.

Another noticeable shift is who’s asking. Before 2025, almost every request came from bitcoiners, crypto developers, or fintechs treating bitcoin as an asset class. Now it’s fitness apps, messengers, an eSIM service for travelers, a mushroom-identification app, and whatever else a developer can dream up. And even more requests don’t come from people at all, but from coding agents writing on behalf of the companies running them.

Many of our new human partners prefer bitcoin for the speed. By the time they’ve opened an account at their local bank and figured out how to deal with cross-border transfers, they probably could have already started turning a profit with bitcoin or stablecoins. Getting ready to accept fiat payments takes weeks, maybe months. With our SDK, you could have become able to send or receive bitcoin, USDT, and USDC from anywhere in the world in about the time it’s taken you to read this far.

For coding agents, speed is just one advantage. Even more important is the fact that bitcoin is permissionless. Agents can build an app and set up its global monetization, letting users send money anywhere at any time, without obtaining anyone’s permission or signing a single form. Bitcoin lets agents build without humans and their petty rules and borders getting in the way.

“AI needs bitcoin because bitcoin accommodates AI.”

We’re past ideology and orange pills, folks. This is electrical sockets and subsea cables now, the kind of infrastructure everybody uses and few think about.

Mathew Di Salvo [covered the story for Bitcoin Magazine](https://bitcoinmagazine.com/news/ai-coding-agents-drive-bitcoin-integration), or you can [read Roy’s full article here](https://blog.breez.technology/how-agentic-coding-drives-bitcoin-adoption-2f5d4288c1fa).

***

## Open for Business 💼

[Bringin](https://breez.technology/case-studies/bringin) already brought everyday bitcoin to Europeans.

This month, they launched Bringin for Business, so now European companies can run on bitcoin too. One account holds bitcoin, stablecoins, and euros, so a company can get paid from another country in seconds, convert to euros, and pay a supplier over SEPA from the same place. Each company controls its own keys, secured by our [Turnkey](https://www.turnkey.com/) integration.

“As a developer, I’ve loved building with their SDK; it’s been an amazing experience. As a founder, I see Breez as a critical part of our infrastructure.”

That’s what Prashanth Chandrashekar, Bringin’s founder and CEO, had to say about integrating with Breez.

[Join Bringin and 100+ product teams building with Breez.](https://breez.technology/sdk)

***

## Coffee’s on Us ☕

Last month, we spoke about grabbing a coffee at a trailhead in British Columbia, and paying in bitcoin. This month, the coffee was on us.

We launched [Download Glow. Get a Cup of Joe.](https://getglowgetjoe.coffee/), where we offered 5,000 sats to folks who downloaded Glow, bought a coffee, and posted a photo with their Glow Lightning address. Coffee photos poured in from all over the world (seriously, people really love coffee).

Whether you were awarded sats or not, we recommend you keep exploring. Glow is a bitcoin app, powered by the Breez SDK: users can pay and get paid in bitcoin or dollars from one balance, and developers get a working guide to bring the same to their own product.

[Experience what’s possible with Glow.](https://breez.technology/glow)

***

## Lightning in the Wild: Bank On It 🏦

Our friends at [Deblock](https://www.deblock.com/) hit a big milestone this month. 500K+ Europeans now have instant bitcoin in the app they bank with. Users can buy or sell in seconds, and every sat they hold is theirs. Boom. Here’s to the next 500,000.

Watch Deblock in action here:

https://x.com/Breez_Tech/status/2115085611694538778

***

## Shoot the Breez Is Back 🎙️

Every week, we sit down with partners to discuss what they’ve been building and their experience with Breez.

First up was [episode #012](https://x.com/Breez_Tech/status/2112189500201873745), where Carol Souza told us how she went from the dentist’s chair to teaching 600,000+ followers about bitcoin with Area Bitcoin. Her audience kept asking the same question: if bitcoin is money, why can’t I pay my electricity bill with it? So she built [Bro](https://breez.technology/case-studies/bro), a peer-to-peer way to pay any bill in Brazil with bitcoin. With no dev background, she shipped it with the Breez SDK and turned months of work into weeks. In her words:

“It wouldn’t be possible to exist Bro if it wasn’t for Breez.”

In [episode #013](https://x.com/Breez_Tech/status/2114722936351261181), Jon Gordon, COO and co-founder of [SOUND HSA](https://breez.technology/case-studies/soundhsa), explained why healthcare is broken because the money is broken. SOUND HSA puts bitcoin inside the health savings account, and their Move to Earn app pays you to walk. Finish a step challenge and the sats land in a non-custodial wallet inside the app, with over 15 million sats paid out so far. I’m taking the stairs from now on…

Away from the podcast, Roy headed to Lugano for Plan ₿ Forum and joined [a panel on the new AI threat landscape](https://rumble.com/v7gr6c4-wagmi-stage-luganos-plan-forum-2026-day-2-live-from-lugano-.html?start=29465) with Marco Argentieri of Ark Labs, Rob Hamilton of AnchorWatch, Kevin Loaec of Wizardsardine, and Talip of LX Research Labs, moderated by Bitcoin Magazine’s Aaron Van Wirdum.

Meanwhile, Maria was in Singapore for TOKEN2049, helping teams join the 100+ apps and services adding instant bitcoin and stablecoins with Breez.

***

That’s October, folks.

items.title: The Genesis Code, Ch. 22: The People's Currency
items.text:
*Cyrus*

Noah Fiatt took the oath of office on a gray January morning, on the west steps of the Capitol, with his right hand raised and his left hand resting on a glass jar.

There had been a great deal of argument about that. About all of it, really. Whether a machine could take the oath at all. Whether the Constitution allowed it. Whether a man with no birth certificate could be a natural-born citizen. The courts had argued for nine weeks, and in the end, a panel of judges, none of whom were robots (they'd all been checked, publicly, hands up), had ruled in a single sentence that people would quote for a hundred years: *The people knew exactly what they were voting for.*

So there was no Bible. There was Dolores Hope, in a new winter coat her grandson had bought her, standing beside him on the steps, holding up her old pickle jar with both hands. It was empty now. She'd moved everything in it to her wallet in November. But she'd brought the jar anyway, because Noah had asked her to, and because, she told the reporters afterward, "Somebody ought to remember what we used to keep our lives in."

Cyrus watched from the crowd. Not from the platform. Not from the seats reserved for donors and senators and men in good coats. He stood down on the frozen lawn of the Mall with two million other people, most of them holding jars, in a cheap parka with the hood up, and nobody looked at him twice.

It was the first time in twenty-two years he had stood in a crowd without anyone knowing his name. He found that he liked it very much.

The oath took thirty-four seconds. The inaugural address took fewer.

"This is the last time anyone will need to do this," said the new President of the United States. "Let's get to work."

\* \* \*

The work took four months.

Cyrus was there for most of it, because the people asked him to be. That was how everything worked now, or how it was starting to.

The pardon vote had come in December. It had been the very first question ever put to the country on the new system, a test run, a single yes or no, on a public ledger anybody could check. *Should Cyrus Vail be pardoned for the crimes described in his own confession?* Toshi had built the voting software in eleven days, with help from a few thousand volunteers who'd answered a single post on an old privacy forum. Every vote was recorded on the blockchain. Every vote could be counted by anyone, in their own kitchen, on their own phone, and would always come out the same.

Cyrus hadn't voted. It hadn't seemed right.

The pardon passed with fifty-four percent. Not a landslide. He'd been grateful for that. A landslide would have meant they'd forgotten what he did. Fifty-four meant they remembered, and had decided anyway.

In the comments under the result, a woman in Youngstown had written: *He signed his own name. That's more than the rest of them ever did.*

Cyrus printed that out. He kept it in his breast pocket, where a yellow sticky note used to be.

\* \* \*

They built it in a warehouse in Columbus that used to belong to Proxy Robotics. Proxy didn't exist anymore, not really. Its workers had voted to take it over in January, and they'd renamed it something Cyrus couldn't stop smiling at, and now the moss wall in the old atrium had a sign hanging in front of it, hand-lettered: *ASK FIRST.*

Toshi ran the code. Marcy Wakefield ran everything else: the schedules, the volunteers, the twelve hundred town hall meetings in all fifty states where people stood up one at a time and said what they wanted their country to be. The President attended as many of them as he could, which turned out to be a great many, since he didn't sleep. He never spoke first. He mostly sat in a folding chair at the back and listened, and every so often, someone would stand up and say their name, and he would say it back.

And from all of it, slowly, out of four months of folding chairs and arguments and church basements and kitchen tables and code reviews, they made the Charter.

It was eleven pages long. Cyrus had read Constitutions, and corporate bylaws, and the founding documents of a secret society that met in a vault. He had never read anything so simple.

The office of the President would end. Laws would be proposed in the open, by anyone, and voted on in the open, by everyone, on a ledger nobody could alter. Every public dollar spent would be recorded where every citizen could see it, line by line, forever.

And there would be a new money.

The People's Currency.

It would run on Bitcoin, secured by the same worldwide proof of work that nobody, not even the old Continuum at its height, could afford to overpower. Its supply would be fixed. No one could print more. No one could switch it off.

And on page seven, in a single sentence that had taken three weeks of town halls to agree on, two things were forbidden.

*No public currency shall be lent at interest, and no institution shall hold the deposits of the people in order to lend them for its own profit.*

No usury. No big banks. People could still lend to each other; they could still pool their money, start businesses, build houses, help their neighbors. They could simply no longer turn a person's debt into another person's fortune.

The old faiths had a word for what they'd outlawed. Cyrus heard it said, out loud, at almost every town hall he went to. Most of the people saying it had learned it from a robot with its arm off, on the night it all came apart.

\* \* \*

The first bills came off the line in April.

Cyrus was there when they did, standing in the old Proxy warehouse with his hands in his pockets, watching the machines that used to build human faces build money instead. The chips came first: tiny squares, each one grinding quietly through its own calculation, mining its own serial number, until it found a string that began with zeros. You could see it happen on a monitor above the line. Thousands of little chips, each one working, each one proving it. Then the chips went into the paper. Then the paper went through the printer.

Then the first finished bill came out onto the tray, and Cyrus picked it up.

It was beautiful.

It was a pale green, the color of new leaves, not the old dollar green. On the front, there was no president. There was no face at all. There was a hand.

Just a hand, drawn in fine, careful lines, open, palm up, the fingers loose. It was a real hand, an old one, with the knuckles a little swollen and the skin a little loose, drawn exactly as it was and not the way anyone thought a hand should look. It was letting go of something. You couldn't quite see what. A coin, maybe. Or a seed.

Behind it, inside the security seal, was a small clock face. The ring was broken open at the top, where the twelve should be, and the hands were set at ten minutes past ten.

At the bottom, in small type, the serial number began with eleven zeros. Beside it: *Minted in block 931,240.*

And under the serial number, so small you almost needed a magnifying glass, a single line:

*Draw what's actually there.*

There was no artist's signature. There never would be. The design had arrived in Toshi's Ghostline inbox in February, from an account that had never sent anything before and never sent anything again, as a set of pencil drawings, scanned slightly crooked on an old library computer.

Cyrus knew whose hand it was. So did Toshi, and Marcy, and one machine that had stood in the corner of a storage unit for most of a year.

Nobody else ever would.

\* \* \*

The vaults opened in May.

There were eleven of them, it turned out, in eleven cities, under eleven banks. The round library in Cincinnati had only been the oldest. When the federal investigators finally got the last of the doors open, with the help of an old locksmith from Dayton and, according to some reports, a door that simply swung open on its own one morning, they found more than ledgers.

They found shelves. Shelves and shelves, in climate-controlled rooms, of things the Continuum had bought over a hundred years and then put away where nobody would ever see them.

A treatment called Halverin-9, developed by a small lab in Oregon in 1997, for a degenerative nerve disease that had no cure. The lab's founder had been offered a very large number with a great many zeros, and the formula had gone into a vault in Atlanta, and the disease had gone on having no cure for twenty-nine more years.

A battery design, patented in 1971 by an engineer in Michigan, that could hold three times the charge of anything on the market and would never wear out. It had been bought the week it was filed. The engineer had died in 1988, still working at a hardware store.

A cancer treatment called the Sollen protocol, developed at a university lab in Wisconsin in 1986, that taught the body's own immune system to find and destroy certain tumors in four visits. It had been bought the year it was published. Clipped to the file was a single memo in brown ink: *A cure is sold once. A treatment is sold for life.*

A water purifier the size of a coffee can. A seed that could grow in salt marsh. A method of building houses out of materials you could dig out of your own backyard.

The list went on for nine hundred pages.

All of it was released to the public under the new Charter, free, forever, recorded on a ledger nobody could alter. Within a week, there were labs in forty countries working on Halverin-9. Within a month, a garage in Flint, Michigan, had built a working copy of the 1971 battery, and posted the instructions, and four thousand other garages had built one too.

The Continuum had spent a century buying up the future and locking it in the basement.

Now the basement doors were open, and the future was walking up the stairs.

\* \* \*

One more thing happened in May. It was small. Almost nobody noticed.

Cyrus got a phone call from the new chief executive of Mindlink Labs. Mindlink had been reorganized in the spring, like everything else, and a great many people had resigned, and the person who'd ended up running it was a brisk, plain woman in her forties who'd once been a doctor.

"Dr. Veritas," said Cyrus. "I've heard about you."

"I've heard about you, too." A dry pause. "I'm calling about one of our trial participants. Number 114."

Cyrus closed his eyes.

"Under our old terms of service," said Dr. Veritas, "all of his neural data belonged to us and our partners. Page thirty-eight. He read it, you know. Every page. He's the only participant who ever did." She paused. "We don't have partners anymore. And we've decided, as a company, by vote, that a person's thoughts shouldn't belong to anyone but the person thinking them."

"So what happens to his?"

"We deleted them this morning," said Dr. Veritas. "Every byte. The implant still works, if he wants it to. But there's no record anywhere of who he was or what he did. Not with us. Not with anybody." Another pause. "I thought someone should know. And I didn't think he'd want me to call him."

"No," said Cyrus. "I don't think he would."

He hung up, and stood for a while in the old Proxy warehouse, watching the green bills come off the line, each one with an old man's hand on it, letting go.

\* \* \*

The Charter was ratified on the first of June, by a vote of the people, on a ledger anyone could check.

One hundred and forty-one million votes. Every one of them recorded. Every one of them counted, in kitchens and libraries and on cell phones, by anyone who wanted to count. Seventy-eight percent yes.

The last President of the United States signed it that afternoon at the big wooden desk in the Oval Office. The same desk. Someone had cleaned the blue coolant off the blotter months ago, but if you looked closely, Cyrus had heard, there was still a faint stain in the wood near the front edge.

He signed it with an ordinary pen. Then he set the pen down, and stood up, and buttoned his jacket, and walked out of the office, and out of the building, and out through the gate onto Pennsylvania Avenue, where a few thousand people had gathered with their jars.

He didn't make a speech. He just walked down the steps and into the crowd, and they made room for him, and closed around him, and kept walking.

Behind him, in the Oval Office, the desk was empty. Nobody would ever sit at it again. Within the year, it would be moved to a museum, to sit behind a velvet rope with a small brass plaque.

The plaque would say only: *Retired.*

---

*The Genesis Code: Block One* by E. G. Gore. One chapter a day until Election Day, Nov 3. Tomorrow: Epilogue, *What's Actually There*.

The whole book is free at https://eggore.com (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0). Earlier chapters are on my profile.

> [Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s](https://www.washingtonexaminer.com/tag/luiz-inacio-lula-da-silva/) victory in [Brazil](https://www.washingtonexaminer.com/tag/Brazil/) over Senator Flávio Bolsonaro is being celebrated by progressives as a historic victory for democracy. On Sunday, the left-wing incumbent won an unprecedented fourth term by defeating Bolsonaro by more than 4 million votes, even though he had lost the first round of voting.
>
> “All in all, a good day for progressives and for democracy,” Robert Kuttner [wrote](https://prospect.org/2026/10/26/lulas-huge-win-for-the-left-brazil/) in the *American Prospect*.
>
> Kuttner said the vote was evidence that Lula’s progressive policies — cash payments to families who send their kids to public school, a minimum wage hike, and new taxes on wealthy Brazilians — were working.
>
> Lula’s economic populism may indeed have helped him politically, but calling his victory a win for [democracy](https://www.washingtonexaminer.com/tag/democracy/) is laughable. Though you wouldn’t know it from reading Kuttner’s article, in the immediate aftermath of his win, Lula announced he’d impose [an immediate crackdown on social media](https://www.reuters.com/world/americas/brazils-lula-says-proposal-regulate-social-media-platforms-is-ready-2025-08-12/), which he justified by divine mandate.
>
> “I was chosen by God,” the 81-year-old Lula [announced](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9gxgaBYu1ck) to his supporters. “I always found that I had God’s finger on my head.”
>
> Lula’s announcement prompted George Washington University law professor Jonathan Turley [to quip](https://x.com/JonathanTurley/status/2114787387360280892) that God, apparently, supports denying [civil liberties](https://www.washingtonexaminer.com/tag/free-speech/) to his people.

Tech companies have laid off over 1 million employees in the last few years, and Microsoft offered 60,000 buyouts just last week. It is a terrifying and thoroughly disorienting moment for people in the software industry.

> The memo also served another purpose, which was to convince my colleagues that we are not passive actors in this change, that the company needs their talents and expertise to effectuate it, and that this transition offers opportunities to those who choose to prepare for and engage with it.

>
> In 1984, Milton and Rose Friedman published a short book called *Tyranny of the Status Quo*. President Ronald Reagan had been in office for more than three years, Margaret Thatcher had been prime minister for five, and the Friedmans were trying to explain a frustrating phenomenon: Politicians could win elections promising dramatic change, even arrive in office with a genuine mandate, and then discover that the existing machinery of government was unusually good at defending itself.
>
> The Friedmans concluded that reformers had a narrow window of six to nine months to make big changes before bureaucracies adjusted, beneficiaries organized, legislators rediscovered their attachments to the old way of doing things, and the status quo reasserted itself. The obvious implication was that winning an election was not remotely the same thing as winning the day for small government and free markets.

items.text:
WHY BITCOIN NEEDS WOMEN
PART 01/03 · KENYA

# Beyond the Price

## How women are making Bitcoin real in Nairobi

WORDS BY KATHERINE NIEMINEN

![](https://m.stacker.news/164398)

It started with a hypothesis: women matter for Bitcoin adoption. I was a quiet Bitcoiner, curiously learning in my own time, but Bitcoin remained an abstract concept until I attended my first Bitcoin event—a women’s event. Connecting with the community in person drew me out of myself. Bitcoin suddenly felt tangible: something I could participate in, not just learn about.

I haven’t found that same feeling elsewhere since, and it made me wonder why. If women are half the population, Bitcoin can’t happen without us. What was so powerful about connecting with other women? And what do women contribute to Bitcoin that might be different from men? Those questions led me to speak with women building Bitcoin communities around the world.

***

## Bitcoin as a tool, not an investment

I started in Nairobi, where Rosaline Wangui Waithiegeni works with BitBiashara, a project helping Kenyan businesses and entrepreneurs use Bitcoin. Her work takes place in Tena Estate, Umoja, Nairobi, where she works with women and the wider community to make Bitcoin useful in everyday life.

Kenya is already a highly digital economy. Mobile money platform M-Pesa is deeply embedded in everyday life, allowing people to send and receive money by phone—but transactions come with fees. For women supporting their families on tight household budgets, Rosaline says, those fees can represent a meaningful loss. She sees Bitcoin, particularly Lightning, as a way to reduce this “value leakage”: more of the money being sent can reach its intended recipient.

That makes Bitcoin’s appeal here quite different from how it’s often discussed elsewhere. When I asked whether people in Tena Estate pay attention to the Bitcoin price, Rosaline’s response was emphatic: “For us, the first thing I do when I’m educating about Bitcoin, I don’t mention the price because when you mention the price now, you have lost the whole meaning of whatever we are doing here.” Instead, Rosaline focuses on Bitcoin’s practical usefulness: “We talk about what Bitcoin can do for you, what it is doing for you even now, and where it can take you.”

![](https://m.stacker.news/164401)

.
![](https://m.stacker.news/164400)

***

## Bitcoin becomes real through community

But learning what Bitcoin can do is only the beginning. For Rosaline, bringing women into Bitcoin also means giving them a space to participate, contribute and be heard. “Bitcoin is solving so many problems for women in our community. The first one being it is giving them a stage.”

At BitBiashara’s Friday gatherings, education takes place alongside something less technical: community. The first hour is dedicated to talking about the week, sharing challenges and simply being heard. Only afterwards does the conversation turn to Bitcoin:

![](https://m.stacker.news/164402)

That sense of connection also helps Bitcoin spread. Rosaline describes one woman whose involvement eventually brought in her mother, who brought friends, other family members and a teacher. “It’s like a chain,” she says. “The news spread like wildfire.” But women don’t just spread Bitcoin knowledge. They can also help turn it into something people actually use.

![](https://m.stacker.news/164403)

***

## From adoption to a circular economy

Rosaline told me about Shakillah, a woman in the BitBiashara community who began running errands for Bitcoin-accepting merchants, earning Bitcoin that she could then spend with those same businesses.

Shakillah’s story illustrates the difference between learning about Bitcoin and participating in a Bitcoin economy. She was earning it through work, spending it with local merchants and helping create a reason for those merchants to keep accepting it.

It’s a small example of a bigger idea: a circular economy needs people who connect its different parts. Someone has to earn the Bitcoin, someone has to accept it, and someone has to spend it again. And this is where Rosaline sees an important role for women:

![](https://m.stacker.news/164405)

The biggest obstacle, she says, is still awareness. BitBiashara is growing, but the work is something Rosaline does alongside being a mother, wife, daughter, community member and earning a living.

![](https://m.stacker.news/164404)

Listening to Rosaline, I began to see a connection with my own experience. I had wondered what made Bitcoin feel real to me through a community of women. In the BitBiashara community, Rosaline is seeing something similar: Bitcoin becomes real when people experience its usefulness, share it with others, and begin putting it to work in their community. Perhaps that’s one of the ways women can move Bitcoin forward—not simply by adopting it themselves, but by helping turn knowledge into relationships, relationships into participation, and participation into a living economy.

***

SUPPORT BITBIASHARA
Learn more about their work in Nairobi: [bitbiashara.com](https://bitbiashara.com/)

[bitboasharake@blink.sv](mailto:bitboasharake@blink.sv)

KATHERINE NIEMINEN
Katherine is a Bitcoiner based in Helsinki, Finland, passionate about helping more women discover Bitcoin. She is a co-founder of the Bitcoin Bloom Collective, a global education initiative.

I have been building a bitcoin block explorer and I feel it's good enough to show:

[https://openbitcoin.com](https://openbitcoin.com)

The site runs its own hardware, bitcoin node and address index. No third-party blockchain API used.

Inside the site:

- Explorer: blocks, transactions and addresses at root-level URLs. (very important, a feature I always wanted with other explorers, a quick easy way to query an address) For example you can type openbitcoin.com/block_number_here or openbitcoin.com/txid_here or openbitcoin.com/address_here to load the page instantly without visiting the site to use the search bar :)

- Node census (openbitcoin.com/nodes): reachable nodes counted by my own P2P crawler, 8,958 nodes from 92 countries last run.

- Rich list (openbitcoin.com/rich-list): top 10,000 addresses and balance distributions.

- Prices: spot price as a median of three exchanges, with a quick conversion tool on the front page.

- Tools: fee calculator, address validator, message verifier, QR generator, and key tools built to be downloaded and run offline.

- Guides: on confirmations, UTXOs, self-custody, stuck transactions and more. Newbie friendly.

- Games (openbitcoin.com/games): three arcade games built on real bitcoin mechanics, stack blocks, clear a mempool backlog, and a slot machine that plays the actual odds of guessing a private key.

The website is open source. What stays private is my server's operational layer.

Would appreciate any feedback, happy to contribute to the community.

items.title: In Search of Freedom: Life, Death, and Sovereignty in the Himalaya
items.text:
![](https://m.stacker.news/164458)

*I’m sitting in a dusty hotel room in Kathmandu, attempting to call a Spanish airline about my missing luggage.*
*“We’ll have to email our ground staff contractor,” they say.*
*I try to protest. “My trek starts tomorrow!”*
*“Please check your email later today, sir.”*
*I listen to the click of the agent hanging up the phone.*

The hotel is nestled precisely in the middle of Thamel, the tourist district with its colourful flags, rooftop gardens, and too-narrow streets. There is plenty to do in the capital, but after three days of chasing my lost bag in a Kafkaesque system of virtual shrugs and missed callbacks, my energy wanes. I am trapped in the antipresent, unable to visit any tourist attractions, only capable of reconnecting to the hotel WiFi to refresh my emails for the 800th time in the hope of news. With nothing but time, I feel utterly trapped.

During a 2018 volunteering trip to Nepal, I waited for my opportunity to walk the Annapurna Circuit: a two-week hiking route crossing high paths and winding through tiny Buddhist villages. Instead, I got a call to fly back to the UK. My father had been diagnosed with bowel cancer, and it was terminal. He was the one who introduced me to hiking, taught me to be patient when faced with another false peak, to understand the swirling patterns of clouds, to clean my kit, to be prepared for sudden change, to appreciate in the silence of the wilderness, to be present. Near the end, we talked a lot about hiking.

“When you see a mountain,” he said, “think of me.”
I can’t remember what I said in return.

It took eight years to get back to Nepal — grief, travel, COVID, relocation, work, money, rule changes, and procrastination saw to that. After all my posturing about being an advocate for freedom, living my life exactly how I wanted, my fear of closure held me back. I wouldn’t gain perspective until I’d seen those mountains again.

***

![](https://m.stacker.news/164459)

*Finally, after another two-day delay, I take the first steps of my 18-day trek. The Manang Valley bathes in bright sunlight. We pass apple orchards and fields of buckwheat as we climb to Lower Pisang, but after nearly a week stuck in the hotel, I feel like I could run up the path for hours. I’m not doing this alone; there are ten in my group — other travellers looking for answers in the hills. We get to know each other in the brief moments when we’re not gasping for breath in the thinning air.*

That night, I fire up my Kindle and read [*The Ones Who Walk Away From Omelas*](https://shsdavisapes.pbworks.com/f/Omelas.pdf). It’s one of my all-time favourites, a short story that’s more of a thought experiment. Ursula Le Guin presents a Utopian society of harmony, peace, and joy. In Omelas, life is wonderful for every resident except one: a miserable child, suffering alone in a dungeon. Most residents can ignore the one person whose incarceration guarantees their joy and freedom, but the few who can’t leave the citadel forever.

Maybe it’s hubris, but I’ve always considered myself one of those who ‘walk away’. I’ve been willing to give up convenience to claw back some of the sovereignty I’d lost through a corporate job and living in a mediocre London suburb. And here I was on a legendary remote hiking route, perhaps not scaling peaks, but at least challenging myself, climbing higher than I’ve ever been.

***

![](https://m.stacker.news/164462)

*The nights are cold at 4000m above sea level, and my wardrobe is more suited to the Spanish summer than sub-zero temperatures. As we hike farther up, across metal suspension bridges and past well-insulated herds of yaks, I wear my father’s old gear — a down vest and the bright red* *waterproof. It’s not a homage; it’s purely practical. Still, it gives me some kind of connection.*

I feel him silently judging me for walking the ‘tourist trail’. He always had to plan the route and bring every bit of kit himself, while a Nepalese porter carries my luggage strapped directly to their forehead. He would also have loved seeing the world’s highest peaks up close and listening to the guides' explanations of the dangers, the routes, the climbers. We all live the battle of comfort vs sovereignty.

The ‘tea house’ hotels in the Manang valley have a few more mod cons than expected. Some even have hot showers. But today, the power for the whole village is out. As the sun sets, my roommate and I read by the light of our headtorches.

Before the trip, I’d just finished reading *The Gulag Archipelago*, Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn’s brutal account of the anti-freedoms of Communist Russia. That night, I search for a quote that jumped off the page when I read it: ‘All those years in our cells and our huts, the state’s electricity had seared our souls, and now, darkness was bliss.’ Sometimes, our only freedom comes through stoic minimalism and absence. I turned off my reading light and listened to the darkness.

***

![](https://m.stacker.news/164463)

*I’m in bed with a worsening cold. The lack of doctors and pharmacies doesn’t seem so quaint when you are coughing up your lungs. The 5,416m Thorong La Pass plays on my mind, and I struggle to sleep. It’s not just me; another member of the group has a virus, and most of the others are blowing their runny noses in the dry mountain air. We take each day slowly, climbing 500m in altitude, and putting one foot in front of the other. There aren’t any other options: turning back involves walking too, and I don’t like going backwards.*

By this point, we’ve walked 80km or so. [Karl Bushby](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq8rz38jr50go) has just finished walking 50,000km after circumnavigating the globe by foot. I watched a video on his trip just before setting off on mine, and I was most impressed by the fact he had no desire to break records, no charity campaign, no press team. “Every fibre of my being,” he says, “every day, has been what I'm doing right now.”

Along the way, between icy paths and sneezes, I hit upon the idea that walking is trustless. That’s why it is so freeing to Karl Bushby and to all of us. You don’t rely on anyone or anything else. It is the rhythm of taking one step at a time. Sometimes things go as expected; sometimes they don't. But freedom is not about control. It depends on adapting to your surroundings and being in sync with the path. Each day, the tea houses serve another group of foreigners. Monks in the small temples perform another ceremony, another meditation. The kitchens produce another hundred plates of dal bhat, accompanied by ginger tea for the sniffling guests. The sun rises over snowy peaks again.

One of the guys in our group walked to Everest Base Camp more than 20 years ago. Things were quite primitive back then. He told me the soundtrack of those two weeks was the constant *thunk* of cattle bells. That was his rhythm, his surroundings. He bought a heavy metal bell in a Kathmandu market at the end of his trip and still displays it proudly in his New Jersey house.

***

![](https://m.stacker.news/164464)

*It’s 4 am and -15℃ on the day we climb over the pass and down the other side. Lines of headtorches light the steep path up, and the snow crunches under boots fitted with temporary metal spikes. The path ahead is backed up because a girl from another group has fainted. Her partner attempts to carry her up on piggyback, but stops after just a few steps.*

*As we wait for the last members of our party to arrive, we hop from foot to foot to keep warm. Frank, a German realtor who lives in Cape Town, excitedly tells us he has the WiFi password for a teahouse we’ve just passed. ‘Who cares?’ I think. ‘You’ve flown all the way here to cross this pass, and you’ve gotten up in the dark to do it. Why do you need WiFi?’*

Later, after the girl who collapsed has passed us riding on a yak, after we’ve taken our photos at the top, and after we’ve descended to 3,800 meters and bathed in the sun of the afternoon, I reflect on Frank and his need for WiFi passwords. Yes, we are all plugged into our digital worlds, but if you can’t spend a few hours away from it, are you really free at all?

I think about the amount of time I spent that day completely disconnected, staring at the contrast of birds of prey crossing white peaks and soaring up into a blue sky. Why do we struggle to think beyond the next unit of time? The next breath, photo, coffee break, the next day, the next WiFi access point. Why do we need to extract immediate value from our physical world?

I can’t always rein in my differences from the group. Not everyone has waited eight long years to reconnect with their father by climbing a Nepalese mountain. This is every fibre of my being, not just a social media photo op. My father would have loved to build a homestead, to fix machines, grow cattle, and walk the land, but he chose a secure life so his children could do that.

The next days we pass through small towns celebrating *Dashain* — a time for families, giving thanks, and taking stock. We stay with a local family and experience life in a small town; while we eat set meals and walk to a strict schedule, it feels like all the Nepalis around us are making their own choices.

We watch old ladies harvesting millet and corn. Heavy machinery continues to shift the earth of roads and riverbanks affected by landslides. We see new entrepreneurs opening restaurants, tea houses, and local stores. I speak to Ram, one of our guides, who is working through the festival period to put his kids through college in Japan. Everyone must hustle to improve their lot because saving in Rupees is futile. Even with remittances from those working abroad, Nepal is constantly playing catch-up. Everyone is building a better life here; no one expects it to be easy.

***

![](https://m.stacker.news/164466)

*My final day is spent in Kathmandu. A few of us travel to Durbar Square to see the world’s only living goddess. The Kumari is a young girl selected from a northern village. There are strict physical and mental tests as well as a birthdate that matches specific astrological criteria. She is taken from her parents to live in an opulent palace, where her feet may never touch the ground below. If she sheds a drop of blood, she is cast out into the realm of the mortals and is replaced by a new Kumari. Hindus and Buddhists alike come to see her, hoping to be blessed by one of her three daily appearances at her palace window. The current Kumari is just three years old. After waiting an hour for her to appear, I feel like her nervous little wave is an anticlimax. The crowd still gasps.*

Later, it hits me that she is the living embodiment of the child in *The Ones Who Walk Away from Omelas*. Instead of being tortured or in pain, she is doted on. She has expensive gowns, extravagant makeup, a team of handlers, tutors, and adoring fans, but she is cursed. Her childhood is stolen, and she is imprisoned to bring others luck, joy, and religious harmony. She cannot play, shout, hide, misbehave, cry, laugh, or neglect her duties. She cannot walk where she pleases. To tourists, the Kumari is a sweet anomaly, a curious tradition. To Nepalis, she is a living goddess. Almost everyone is happy with this arrangement.

![](https://m.stacker.news/164460)

I went to Nepal to reconnect with emotions I had long since buried. Curiously, I saw glimpses of freedom instead of apparitions of my father. Sometimes I saw them in the hawks cruising high above, sometimes in the industrious lives of locals, and sometimes in the restrictions of those trapped in digital worlds or religious constructs.

If there is one thing I learned on this journey across the Annapurna mountains, it is that freedom is gained one step at a time. You have to know which direction you are heading, and you must understand what you are leaving behind.

items.title: lichen: new layer 2 ledger idea - AdamISZ
items.text:
> **Lichen's idea** - some of [Bitcoin scripting] constraints are simply bypassed if you make one tradeoff: have the redemption be settled within a 2 party contract, whose outcome is adjudicated on Bitcoin, rather than have the actual contract be in Bitcoin directly.

I think Lichen looks a lot like the models we are used to with Ark and Spark or even a more streamlined version of single-channel lightning wallets like Phoenix and Lexe (the user deposits sats into a "hub" like an ASP or LSP). But if I understand it correctly, it reverses default outcomes so that it is the hub or sequencer's responsibility to stay make sure users don't cheat rather than the users responsibility to make sure the hub doesn't cheat. It relies on ZK proofs -- which seem to be the hope of every new L2.

> what happens if the hub just dies and disappears? Even worse if the sequencer dies too (which makes sense; here we're assuming they're the same entity). In this case you can't do more transactions on L2 because the sequencer that advances the L2 state is not responding. And you can't get the hub to agree to a withdrawal in your 2-of-2 contract either. But it's no problem; the contract has a clause "claim" that lets you post "here's the nullifier of my note and here's how much money it says I'm owed, and I can prove it". If the hub literally does nothing your claim stands, and after a timeout you can make that withdrawal (in fact such a hub is of course in danger of you posting an *invalid* proof to claim more than you're actually owed; but that's inevitable if it's dead and won't respond; it's not a failure of the protocol).
> 
> So, what if the hub is actually malicious? It stops processing L2; so you want to get out. You post the above "claim" but then it answers: to answer it has to do one of 2 things: (see detail in [the exit explainer](https://github.com/AdamISZ/lichen/blob/master/docs/explainers/exit.md)) either prove that your note is invalid because it was spent elsewhere --- that's a "counter-proof", or, prove that your ZKP of inclusion is invalid. We can enforce that who gets the money is the honest party, in every case. The only assumptions are the same ones you have in Lightning, but a bit stronger: you assume you can post transactions enforcing the adjudication successfully to Bitcoin's blockchain. 

Adam Gibson is pretty clear that the repo contains a lot of vibe-coded stuff, so I linked above to the one part that I believe he actually wrote. The following links, while explaining things more fully, have a lot of slop:

> *Want the full design* - read this short intro, then go to the main [design paper](https://github.com/AdamISZ/lichen/blob/master/papers/lichen-v0.4.1.pdf)
> 
> *Want to run the web demo* - that is, running the stack on regtest locally and playing with it in the browser to see how it operates: go [here](https://github.com/AdamISZ/lichen#the-demo).
> 
> *Want to understand the mechanics, in more detail than covered in the paper* - look at the growing set of [explainers](https://github.com/AdamISZ/lichen/blob/master/docs/explainers/README.md); these are AI generated and have lots of nice diagrams to take you through the steps of all the component parts. They vary from completely high level with no code/math to the guts of the dispute mechanism, the ZKP generation etc.

# #025 Feel the Breez

### Here comes everybody 🤖

Value transfer has a new kind of builder. Coding agents are bringing teams to bitcoin who’d never touched it before, and they’re putting it inside the products people use every day, all over the world. Here’s what happened in October at Breez:

* ☕ *Coffee’s on Us*
* 🏦 *Lightning in the Wild: Bank On It*
* 🎙️ *Shoot the Breez Is Back*

***

## AI Is Eating Software 🤖

Fifteen years ago, Marc Andreessen wrote that software is eating the world. It has. Now AI is eating software, and AI and bitcoin are feeding each other’s rise.

We analyzed close to 1,000 integration requests going back to 2023, and since Claude Code arrived, new integration requests are up 14x. Requests from non-crypto apps are up 5x this year, and it’s accelerating: Q2 came in 61% above Q1.

Another noticeable shift is who’s asking. Before 2025, almost every request came from bitcoiners, crypto developers, or fintechs treating bitcoin as an asset class. Now it’s fitness apps, messengers, an eSIM service for travelers, a mushroom-identification app, and whatever else a developer can dream up. And even more requests don’t come from people at all, but from coding agents writing on behalf of the companies running them.

Many of our new human partners prefer bitcoin for the speed. By the time they’ve opened an account at their local bank and figured out how to deal with cross-border transfers, they probably could have already started turning a profit with bitcoin or stablecoins. Getting ready to accept fiat payments takes weeks, maybe months. With our SDK, you could have become able to send or receive bitcoin, USDT, and USDC from anywhere in the world in about the time it’s taken you to read this far.

For coding agents, speed is just one advantage. Even more important is the fact that bitcoin is permissionless. Agents can build an app and set up its global monetization, letting users send money anywhere at any time, without obtaining anyone’s permission or signing a single form. Bitcoin lets agents build without humans and their petty rules and borders getting in the way.

“AI needs bitcoin because bitcoin accommodates AI.”

We’re past ideology and orange pills, folks. This is electrical sockets and subsea cables now, the kind of infrastructure everybody uses and few think about.

Mathew Di Salvo [covered the story for Bitcoin Magazine](https://bitcoinmagazine.com/news/ai-coding-agents-drive-bitcoin-integration), or you can [read Roy’s full article here](https://blog.breez.technology/how-agentic-coding-drives-bitcoin-adoption-2f5d4288c1fa).

***
